items.title: The Life and Death of Stars that Capture Primordial Black Holes
items.abstract: Primordial black holes (PBHs) in the asteroid mass window (10 17 –10 23 g) remain viable dark matter candidates and can be captured by stars. We develop the first global framework for the evolution of stars that capture PBHs, combining analytic calculations, stellar evolution models, 3D general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations, and Monte Carlo population synthesis. We find that the fate of these systems bifurcates: PBHs that form an accretion disk before consuming the host drive explosive disruption, whereas PBHs captured too late or growing too slowly consume the star quietly. Capture is dominated by three-body interactions with planetary or stellar companions. For a solar-type host with a Jupiter analog, inspiral within a main-sequence lifetime requires M BH crit ≳ 1 0 22 g , while lighter PBHs generally require tighter companions. Once deposited at the center, the PBH grows through inefficient quasi-spherical Bondi accretion; if it reaches the angular-momentum threshold before consuming the host, the inflow circularizes into a disk. Our Monte Carlo calculations yield sizable quiet-consumption and explosive-disruption populations, with final PBH masses M BH ∼ 0.01–1 M ⊙ and disk-forming PBH spins a * ≈ 0.8. Disk formation is the point of no return: disk winds and relativistic jets of ∼10 45 –10 50 erg s −1 disrupt the star within minutes. The resulting transients may include a ∼day-long UV/blue signal, radio afterglow, and, if the jet escapes, an X-ray-flash (XRF)/low-luminosity gamma-ray-burst (llGRB) signal. For an O ( 1 ) PBH dark matter fraction and optimistic capture assumptions, the event rate can reach that of llGRBs. The low-mass, high-spin remnants offer a complementary PBH probe and possible source for subsolar black hole mergers.

items.title: Majorana fermions at self-generated interfaces
items.abstract: The Kitaev model describing a one-dimensional topological superconducting chain is known to support two Majorana fermions localized at the endpoints of the system when the parameters are tuned to the topological phase. In this work, we investigate the possibility that Majorana fermions may also emerge away from the physical boundaries of the chain. To this end, we generalize the Kitaev model by incorporating a local coupling between the electronic density and a classical elastic (lattice) field. This electron-lattice interaction can drive phase separation between superconducting regions characterized by distinct topological invariants, thereby generating internal interfaces that host Majorana bound states. Under these conditions, a dilute gas of Majorana fermions can emerge spontaneously in the bulk of the system, without the need for externally imposed interfaces.

items.title: Investigating black hole accretion and feedback self-regulation in Seyfert galaxies using the FIRE-3 cosmological hydrodynamic simulations
items.abstract: Observations of local Seyfert galaxies show an intriguing connection between AGN luminosity and a deficit of molecular gas on ∼50 pc scales compared to 200 pc, the plausible imprint of AGN feedback. Motivated by these findings, we investigate the interplay between supermassive black hole (BH) accretion, AGN feedback, and nuclear gas reservoirs using cosmological hydrodynamic simulations implementing FIRE-3 multi-phase interstellar medium (ISM) physics and multi-component BH accretion and feedback models. Focusing on the late-time evolution of four Milky Way-mass galaxies, we find recurrent cycles of increased gas inflow toward the accretion disc, enhanced BH accretion, feedback self-regulation, and suppressed gas inflow rate until the next fuelling event. AGN winds interact with the ISM and escape preferentially through low-density polar channels after opening central cavities on ∼10–500 pc scales, regulating BH growth and producing episodic behaviour on ∼10–100 Myr timescales. The simulations reproduce the observed diversity of nuclear morphologies, gas concentrations, and AGN luminosities in late-type Seyfert galaxies, but do not exhibit a clear anti-correlation between gas concentration and AGN luminosity. Higher-luminosity AGN (LX ∼ 1041.5 − 43 erg s−1) powered by the accretion disc reservoir can coexist with feedback-driven cavities, consistent with observations, but they are more common in simulated galaxies with centrally-peaked gas distributions. Although differences in sample selection, tracer choice, spatial resolution, and stochasticity in AGN fuelling may impact underlying concentration-luminosity trends, the apparent tension between simulations and observations points to the timing between gas inflow, accretion-disc depletion, and feedback-driven clearing on ∼50–200 pc scales as a key constraint on AGN self-regulation models.

items.title: Improving the Precision of Line-by-line Radial Velocities: A Data-driven Iterative Algorithm for Spectral Line Selection
items.abstract: Independent analysis of individual spectral lines, or line-by-line (LBL) analyses, can improve upon standard cross-correlation function (CCF) methods for measuring radial velocities (RVs) because they preserve critical information about individual line-shape changes that can be caused by stellar activity. In this work, we measure LBL RVs of 3830 spectral lines across 383 days of NEID solar observations. Our LBL approach achieves an RV rms of 2.012 m s −1 using all lines. Then, we describe several benchmark methods to select smaller line lists based on line properties such as depth and intrinsic RV scatter. Our primary finding is that a smaller line list can result in higher-quality and more stable RVs than standard RV extraction approaches. Motivated by these results, we present Filtering Lines for Accurate Radial-velocity Exoplanet Search (FLARES), an iterative line-selection algorithm. FLARES selects candidate spectral lines with extreme values of multiple line metrics and properties such as depth, signal-to-noise ratio, and detector position, and preferentially rejects lines whose removal produces the largest decrease in the weighted RV scatter. We find that FLARES-selected line lists can substantially reduce the RV rms with substantially fewer lines, outperforming the full line list and benchmark line-selection methods. Cross-validation tests demonstrate that FLARES is robust, yielding an RV rms of ≈1.3 m s −1 using just ≈25−100 lines. Comparisons to alternative line lists with properties similar to the best FLARES-selected lines demonstrate that FLARES successfully identifies line properties that lead to effective line lists for future extreme-precision radial velocity measurements.

items.title: Neutron stars with an agnostic dark sector: Core and halo configurations from a two-fluid approach
items.abstract: The study of dark matter admixed neutron stars has the potential to advance our understanding of dark matter particle candidates. However, the large parameter space of dark matter particle masses restricts a systematic, model-independent study. In this analysis, we employ agnostic hadronic and dark-matter equations of state to construct dark-matter-admixed neutron stars within a two-fluid formalism. Dark matter is characterized solely by its low-density equation of state and mass and is modeled as a Fermi gas, while hadronic matter is anchored at low and high densities by chiral effective field theory and perturbative quantum chromodynamics calculations. A speed-of-sound parametrization describes the intermediate- and high-density regimes of both hadronic and dark matter, enabling an agnostic treatment of the dark matter equation of state that is constrained only by thermodynamic consistency and does not favor softer or stiffer behavior. Within this agnostic framework, we find that dark matter does not generically compactify the star: light dark matter forms extended halos that raise the tidal deformability, while heavy dark matter forms compact cores that lower it. Consequently, the dominant observational constraint shifts from gravitational-wave tidal deformability for light, halo-dominated models to NICER mass-radius data for heavy, core-dominated models. Using current data at 1 σ , we constrain the dark matter fraction to f D M ≲ 0.11 for light dark matter. By treating the medium- and high-density dark matter equation of state agnostically within a fermionic framework, our approach yields conservative and broadly applicable bounds on the dark matter content of neutron stars. Neutron stars with similar masses but very different tidal deformabilities could be a smoking-gun signature of dark matter in Neutron stars.

items.title: Charting the expansion of the Universe from z∼0 to z∼14 with HII galaxies
items.abstract: We present an updated Hubble diagram of giant extragalactic H ii regions and H ii galaxies spanning the redshift interval z ∼ 0 to z ∼ 14, extending the use of the L(Hβ) − σ relation as an independent cosmological probe into the epoch of cosmic dawn. Our sample comprises 243 objects, including local anchor systems with primary distance measurements, previously published low- and intermediate-redshift H ii galaxies, recent JWST/NIRSpec observations, and a new subsample of extremely high-redshift H ii galaxies observed with JWST and, for the highest-redshift cases, with ALMA+JWST. We homogenise the measurements across the full sample, applying consistent corrections for instrumental and thermal broadening, extinction, and, where required, the transformation from [O III]-based to Balmer-line velocity dispersions. We model lensing effects of high redshift using a log-normal magnification formalism and infer cosmological parameters via a nested-sampling analysis, considering both spatially flat and non-flat versions of the ΛCDM, wCDM, and CPL models. The L − σ relation remains consistent over the full redshift range, showing no evidence for significant evolution even at the highest redshifts currently accessible. For the joint anchor+H ii galaxies sample, considering the spatially flat models, we obtain h = 0.725 ± 0.040 and $\Omega _m=0.308^{+0.043}_{-0.053}$ for ΛCDM. Allowing a constant dark-energy equation of state yields $w_0=-0.96^{+0.53}_{-0.21}$, while a CPL parametrisation gives $w_0=-0.92^{+0.57}_{-0.34}$ and $w_a=-0.48^{+0.60}_{-1.50}$, all consistent, within the uncertainties, with concordance cosmology. These results demonstrate that H ii galaxies offer a viable, fully independent tracer of the expansion history across almost the entire age of the Universe, opening a new avenue for testing ΛCDM and dark-energy evolution well beyond reionisation.

items.title: Primordial black holes and gravitational waves as multimessenger signals of first-order phase transitions
items.abstract: The collapse of false-vacuum domains during first-order phase transitions in the early Universe may lead to primordial black hole (PBH) formation whose signatures form a multimessenger complement to gravitational wave (GW) production. We focus on PBH formation through the gravitational collapse of false-vacuum domains, described using a junction condition formalism. This formalism develops the Schwarzschild collapse criterion dynamically, avoiding the usage of critical overdensity thresholds in a post-inflationary Universe, and is driven solely by the vacuum energy enclosed within shrinking false-vacuum domains without the assistance of particle or domain wall interactions in the false vacuum. We study the parameter space of phase transitions and identify regions producing observable GWs, observable PBHs, or both simultaneously. We investigate this phenomenology in polynomial and classically conformal scalar field potentials as model benchmarks. We find that the scalar fields with vacuum expectation values in the range of 1-100 MeV have the largest model parameter space available for these multi-messenger signals, which are testable with upcoming GW observatories, searches for Hawking radiation, and gravitational lensing surveys.

items.title: Monopoles, strings, walls, and gravitational waves
items.abstract: The gauge symmetry breaking S U ( 2 ) → U ( 1 ) → Z 2 → 1 successively produces monopoles, strings and domain walls bounded by strings (WBS), with the elementary monopole carrying a U ( 1 ) magnetic flux twice as large as the elementary string. The elementary strings and subsequently WBS emit gravitational waves, and during their decay, the WBS yield a network of composite strings that carry the same U ( 1 ) flux as the monopoles. Depending on the cosmological evolution, we provide the gravitational wave spectra generated by the elementary strings and WBS, in combination with the composite strings which are either effectively stable, quasistable, or metastable. These three scenarios are also realized in the symmetry breaking chain S U ( 3 ) → S O ( 3 ) → Z 2 → 1 . Both S U ( 2 ) and S U ( 3 ) have appeared in the literature as flavor gauge symmetries.

items.title: A Calibration Database Design for the Wide-field X-ray Telescope on Board the Einstein Probe
items.abstract: The wide-field X-ray telescope (WXT) is the primary payload of the Einstein Probe mission. Utilizing innovative lobster-eye micro-pore optics, it achieves an unprecedented combination of a large instantaneous field-of-view and high detection sensitivity. Precise scientific data analysis relies fundamentally on a standardized and robust calibration database (CALDB). In this paper, we present the design and implementation of the WXT CALDB. The database is designed to manage calibration data for 12 independent WXT modules and 48 complementary metal-oxide semiconductor sensors, incorporating both extensive on-ground calibration results and dynamic in-orbit updates. We detail the directory hierarchy, naming conventions, functionality, and the specific formats of key calibration products. The WXT CALDB is seamlessly integrated into the WXT data analysis pipeline, ensuring high data integrity and maximizing the scientific return of the mission.

items.title: Entropic Chaplygin-gas cosmology and late-universe tension diagnostics
items.abstract: We investigate an entropic generalized Chaplygin-gas (gCg) cosmology in which a single dark fluid accounts for both dark matter and dark energy. We constrain the model using DESI baryon acoustic oscillations, redshift-space-distortion measurements, compressed Planck 2018 distance and lensing information, and Type Ia supernova likelihoods with PantheonPlus+SH0ES (PPS) and DES–Dovekie. For Planck+DESI+RS D+PPS, the entropic gCg model yields $$H_{0}=68.64\pm 0.52,\mathrm{km,s^{-1},Mpc^{-1}}$$ H 0 = 68.64 ± 0.52 , km , s - 1 , Mpc - 1 and $$S_{8}=0.797\pm 0.021$$ S 8 = 0.797 ± 0.021 , compared with $$H_{0}=67.31\pm 0.28,\mathrm{km,s^{-1},Mpc^{-1}}$$ H 0 = 67.31 ± 0.28 , km , s - 1 , Mpc - 1 and $$S_{8}=0.809\pm 0.021$$ S 8 = 0.809 ± 0.021 in $$\Lambda $$ Λ CDM. The simultaneous upward shift in $$H_{0}$$ H 0 and downward shift in $$S_{8}$$ S 8 occurs in the directions required for a partial alleviation of both tensions. We also show that when PPS is replaced by DES–Dovekie, the parameter shifts are smaller, the best-fit improvement is negligible, and the Bayesian evidence favours $$\Lambda $$ Λ CDM. Thus, the entropic gCg model provides a potentially interesting simultaneous shift of $$H_{0}$$ H 0 and $$S_{8}$$ S 8 , but its statistical support depends on the adopted supernova likelihood.

items.title: An engineered nanobody inhibitor for molecular-to-circuit control of opioid receptors.
items.abstract: Opioid receptors (ORs) orchestrate pain relief, reward and dependence, yet their signaling across diverse cell types and subcellular compartments cannot be resolved by current pharmacological or genetic approaches. Single-domain antibodies, or nanobodies (Nbs), can probe receptor states, but their potential for controlling native receptor signaling at the systems level remains unexplored. Here we engineer high-affinity intracellular Nbs that bind active ORs through structure-guided evolution. Iterative functional optimization yields Nb64, an active-state-selective inhibitor that rapidly suppresses transducer engagement, receptor internalization and downstream signaling, including native μOR-driven G protein-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium currents in ventral tegmental area neurons. Organelle targeting enables precise subcellular control of OR signaling, while bioreversible cell-penetrating peptide conjugation enables nongenetic cytosolic delivery. Cell-type-specific Nb64 expression in ventral tegmental area GABAergic neurons attenuates fentanyl-evoked dopamine release and behavioral responses in mice. Nb64 provides a versatile strategy for dissecting OR biology and establishes a generalizable framework for precision inhibition of native G protein-coupled-receptor signaling in vivo.

items.title: Brain extracellular matrix remodelling in health and neuropsychiatric disorders.
items.abstract: The neural extracellular matrix (ECM) is increasingly recognized as an active regulator of brain function and an important contributor to the pathogenesis of neuropsychiatric disorders. This Review examines ECM organization, function and adaptive remodelling in the healthy brain and synthesizes evidence for its pathophysiological alterations in schizophrenia, major depressive disorder and bipolar disorder. Based on findings from human studies and animal models, we propose an ECM-extended conceptual framework of major psychiatric diseases in which polygenic liability, stress exposure and neuroinflammatory signalling converge to remodel the ECM in circuits supporting reward processing, emotion regulation, cognitive control and social cognition. In this model, an early phase of protease-dominant ECM loosening destabilizes microcircuits composed of parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory neurons and principal cells whereas later reactive ECM rebuilding stabilizes dysfunctional network states and contributes to disease persistence, relapse and treatment resistance. This framework positions the ECM as a central hub of genetic, glial, synaptic and systems-level pathogenesis and suggests avenues for the development of ECM-sensitive biomarkers and ECM-directed interventions that may improve the treatment of these disorders.

items.title: Factors associated with transmission of Mediterranean diet from mothers to children and maintaining it during childhood in the mother-child INMA cohort study.
items.abstract: The Mediterranean diet (MD) promotes metabolic health and development, but evidence on its intergenerational transmission remains limited. This study aimed to assess the association between maternal adherence to the MD during pregnancy and offspring MD adherence at 4 and 8 years, and to identify sociodemographic and lifestyle-associated factors of its maintenance. We conducted cross-sectional analyses of 1770 mother-child pairs at 4 years and 1497 at 8 years within the INfancia y Medio Ambiente (INMA) mother-child cohort study. Maternal and child Mediterranean diet adherence at ages 4 and 8 years was assessed using validated food frequency questionnaires and then used to calculate the relative Mediterranean diet score (0-16). Adherence was categorized as low (0-6), intermediate (7-10), or high (11-16), and as non-adherent (0-6) or adherent (7-16). Children were classified into four categories according to their maintenance of adherence between 4 and 8 years as adherence, loss of adherence, improved adherence, and no adherence. Linear, logistic, and multinomial regression models were applied to estimate adjusted regressions coefficients (ß), odds ratios (OR), and relative risks ratios (RRR), respectively, and their 95% confidence intervals (95%CI). Children of adherent mothers (7-16 points) had higher odds of being adherent at 4 years (OR = 1.72; 95% CI 1.36-2.18), and at 8 years (OR = 1.73; 95% CI 1.33-2.26). Children of mothers with high adherence (score 11-16) showed higher adherence at 4 (RRR = 4.69; 95% CI 2.90-7.59) and at 8 years (RRR = 2.05; 95% CI 1.22-3.43). The maintenance of child MD adherence from 4 to 8 years was positively associated with maternal adherence and educational level, and negatively with higher television viewing time. Conclusion This study shows that higher maternal adherence to the MD during pregnancy was associated with higher MD adherence in offspring at ages 4 and 8 years, although more studies should confirm these results and the role of other factors. What is known • The Mediterranean diet has been linked to health benefits and child development. • Family environment is key to consolidating healthy dietary habits in childhood that persist over time, but evidence the intergenerational transmission of the Mediterranean diet from mother to off spring remains limited. What is new • Higher maternal Mediterranean diet adherence during pregnancy was associated with higher off spring adherence at 4 and 8 years. • Maintenance of the child's adherence to the Mediterranean diet between 4 and 8 years was positively associated with maternal adherence and educational level, and negatively with higher television viewing.

items.title: Scalable electron tomography for connectomics.
items.abstract: We demonstrate limited-tilt, serial-section electron tomography (ET), which can non-destructively map brain circuits over large 3D volumes and provide high-resolution, supramolecular details within subvolumes of interest. Here we show accelerated ET imaging of semi-thick sections ( >500 nm) from the mouse cerebellar cortex, with 3D resolution <15 nm and machine learning-based image augmentation, providing the capacity to resolve key features of neuronal circuits including chemical synapses, endocytic structures and gap junctions. Furthermore, we systematically assess how imaging parameters affect image quality and speed to enable connectomic-scale projects.

items.title: A state-dependent glymphatic dimension in major depressive disorder: implications for treatment resistance.
items.abstract: The glymphatic system refers to cerebrospinal fluid-interstitial fluid exchange and proposed drainage pathways shaped by sleep, arousal, vascular dynamics, and astrocytic organization. This physiology offers a way to connect disturbances that often coexist in major depressive disorder (MDD): disrupted sleep, fatigue, cognitive slowing, and stress-related abnormalities. We propose that difficulty establishing or maintaining a coordinated sleep-astrocyte-vascular state may contribute to illness persistence in some patients. Treatment-resistant depression (TRD) provides a setting in which this possibility can be examined across the course of treatment. Preclinical studies link stress and depressive-like behavior to astrocytic injury, aquaporin-4 dysregulation, and altered fluid transport. Human imaging findings vary across depressive phenotypes. In a dedicated TRD study, a higher diffusion tensor imaging along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) ratio was partly driven by reduced denominator diffusivity, illustrating the importance of interpreting this indirect index at component level. Whole-brain spatiotemporal models provide a complementary account of the neural activity accompanying these physiological states. Ketamine/esketamine, transcranial magnetic stimulation, and chronobiological interventions offer different ways to investigate treatment-related change; serotonergic psychedelics provide an exploratory extension. Longitudinal studies can establish how changes in sleep, fluid-sensitive imaging, and neural dynamics relate temporally to clinical recovery. This Perspective therefore develops a potentially modifiable physiological dimension of persistent depressive illness and defines how it can be tested.

items.title: Dosage compensation is regulated by segregated chromatin modules during development in Drosophila.
items.abstract: Dosage compensation (DC) restores the expression balance between the X chromosome and autosomes in males. How this chromosome-wide regulation is precisely regulated to accommodate the heterogeneous functions and dosage-sensitivity among X-linked genes is unclear. To address this, we analyse the epigenomic and 3D genome data of mostly sexed samples from embryos to adults of Drosophila melanogaster, whose DC is known to be mediated by three classes of X-enriched sequence elements of HAS/CES, PionX and 1.688 3F satellites. We find that about 30% of the X-linked genes are compensated specifically in one or a few male stages or tissues, indicated by their significant bindings of the DC-associated protein or H4K16ac histone modification. These specifically (SDC) or facultatively (FDC) compensated genes are more likely to have a developmentally regulated expression and a highly relevant function with the stage or tissue where they are compensated. They show a higher level of co-binding of facultative heterochromatin hallmark H3K27me3 than the constitutively (CDC) compensated housekeeping genes. CDC genes preferentially harbor constitutive long-range (>1Mb) contacts (LRCs) with other CDC genes and the HAS elements, which form by the onset of DC in embryos. While SDC and FDC genes show developmentally increased LRCs with the respective type of genes and the PionX elements and 1.688 3F satellites. The CDC genes and their interacting partners more often coincide with the constitutive boundaries of topologically associated domains, while the other DC genes tend to coincide with the developmentally regulated boundaries. Our results uncover that the Drosophila DC is regulated through separate chromatin modules between housekeeping vs. developmental genes involving different combinations of regulatory sequence elements and 3D genome contacts. This provides broad implications for the hierarchical regulation of DC against different developmental and gene backgrounds among other organisms.

items.title: A reproducible structural brain axis of alcohol use severity.
items.abstract: Alcohol use is linked to distributed structural brain alterations, but population-level alcohol-related neurobiology remains difficult to quantify. We tested whether deep learning-derived MRI representations capture reproducible variation in alcohol consumption severity and converge with clinical and biological markers. Representations were extracted from gray-matter volume maps in the German National Cohort (NAKO; N ≈ 28,000). Ridge-regression scores were derived from structural MRI to estimate alcohol consumption severity, measured with the Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test-Consumption (AUDIT-C). Models were trained in NAKO, externally validated in UK Biobank (N ≈ 25,000), evaluated in FOR2107 (N ≈ 1900), and tested against ICD-10 alcohol use disorder (AUD), alcohol-related biomarkers, and cognition. In NAKO, the structural MRI-derived ridge-regression score correlated with measured AUDIT-C severity (r = 0.11; 95% CI, 0.09-0.12; q FDR = 1.2 × 10 -70 ; MAE = 1.64). This association replicated in UK Biobank (r = 0.09; 95% CI, 0.07-0.10; q FDR = 4.9 × 10 -41 ; MAE = 1.96) and generalized to AUD, with higher odds in the highest versus lowest brain-score quintile (OR = 2.28; 95% CI, 1.49-3.48; q FDR = 3.9 × 10 -4 ). The score was associated with gamma-glutamyl transferase (β = 1.17 U/L; q FDR = 0.007), mean corpuscular volume (β = 14.26 fL; q FDR = 4.4 × 10 -4 ), and slower reaction time (β = 163.40 ms; q FDR = 3.0 × 10 -5 ). Deep learning-derived structural MRI representations capture weak but reproducible alcohol-related brain variation that converges with AUD diagnosis, peripheral biomarkers, and cognition, supporting their use in population-level addiction neuroscience while underscoring limits for individual-level prediction.

items.title: Cortical Hypoperfusion in Acute Anorexia Nervosa Is Graded Along the Sensorimotor-Association Hierarchy.
items.abstract: Objective Cortical gray-matter changes in anorexia nervosa (AN) are among the largest reported in psychiatry, but the functional-metabolic state of that tissue is largely unknown. Because cortical energy use is highest in transmodal association cortex (prefrontal, parietal, and temporal regions of the default-mode and frontoparietal networks), a reduced energy supply predicts a graded rather than uniform reduction in perfusion (blood delivery to tissue). Method A total of 44 acutely underweight women with AN and 45 healthy women underwent 3 T pseudo-continuous arterial spin labeling with partial-volume correction. Cerebral blood flow was compared between groups across the Schaefer 100 regions 7 networks atlas, age-adjusted and false-discovery-rate-corrected, and the case-control map was compared with the principal functional gradient (the axis running from sensorimotor to transmodal cortex), with cortical thickness in the same participants, and with 18 PET and SPECT receptor maps. Results Perfusion was lower in AN in 97 of 100 regions and maximal in orbitofrontal and prefrontal cortex (composite d = -0.56). The deficit scaled with position along the principal functional gradient (ρ = -0.56), an axis unrelated to perfusion in health, and was recoverable in individual brains (d = -0.53). Thinning was widespread but unrelated to gradient position, and the two effect maps did not correspond. Hypoperfusion was greater where D1, CB1, mGluR5, M1, 5-HT2A, and μ-opioid systems are dense, the dopaminergic, cannabinoid, glutamatergic, and muscarinic ones persisting after gradient adjustment. Discussion Cortical perfusion in acute AN is not uniformly reduced but organized along the cortex's principal functional axis, dissociable from cortical thinning and aligned with reward-related neurochemistry.

items.title: International Expert Consensus Statement on Contemporary Prevention and Management of Postoperative Delirium in Cardiac Surgery.
items.abstract: Background Postoperative delirium is among the most frequent neurocognitive complications of cardiac surgery, with reported incidence ranging from 14% to more than 50% depending on patient population and operative complexity. It is independently associated with prolonged mechanical ventilation, extended intensive care unit and hospital stay, long-term cognitive decline, and increased mortality. Despite this burden, prevention and management strategies remain inconsistent across institutions worldwide. Methods An international multidisciplinary expert panel applied a structured PICOT (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, Timing) framework to predefined clinical questions spanning four perioperative phases: preoperative, intraoperative, postoperative and intensive care, and recovery after intensive care. Designated expert groups synthesized available evidence through structured literature reviews, and consensus recommendations were developed using a modified Delphi methodology. Results The panel developed 14 consensus statements. Preoperatively, routine screening with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment and Clinical Frailty Scale, and multicomponent optimization are recommended. Opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia is recommended, whereas perioperative dexmedetomidine in place of benzodiazepines, cerebral oximetry, processed electroencephalography-guided anesthesia depth monitoring, and optimized oxygen delivery may be considered. In intensive care, validated delirium screening paired with sedation assessment, daily awakening and breathing trials, structured multicomponent care bundles, correction of reversible precipitants, and circadian-supportive environments are central. After transfer from intensive care, continued ward screening and structured post-discharge cognitive follow-up are recommended. Conclusions These statements provide a framework for preventing and managing postoperative delirium after cardiac surgery and advocate a coordinated multimodal approach. Standardizing screening, prevention bundles, and long-term follow-up within routine clinical pathways is recommended as a core institutional priority.

items.title: Dietary sodium restriction enhances the renoprotective efficacy of endothelin-A receptor antagonism in proteinuric chronic kidney disease.
items.abstract: Introduction Endothelin-A receptor antagonists (ERAs) are emerging as an important treatment for proteinuric chronic kidney disease (CKD). As with renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) inhibition, dietary sodium intake may influence their therapeutic efficacy, but this has not been investigated. Here, we examined whether dietary sodium restriction enhances the systemic and kidney effects of acute selective endothelin-A (ETA) receptor antagonism in proteinuric CKD. Methods In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study, 12 adults (mean age 46 years) with non-diabetic proteinuric CKD (mean eGFR 55 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ; median proteinuria 1.8 g/day) receiving maximally tolerated RAAS inhibition completed two 14-day dietary interventions (habitual dietary sodium intake [13.3 g salt/day] and dietary sodium restriction [6.3 g salt/day, approximating guideline-recommended levels]) in random order. During each dietary period, participants underwent two study visits and received intravenous infusion of either placebo or the selective ET A receptor antagonist, BQ123. Systemic hemodynamics, arterial stiffness, kidney hemodynamics and proteinuria were assessed following each intervention. Results BQ123 produced comparable reductions in systolic blood pressure (about 12-14 mmHg), systemic vascular resistance and arterial stiffness under both dietary conditions and increased kidney blood flow (about 320-335 mL/min) irrespective of dietary sodium intake. In contrast, significant reductions in glomerular filtration rate (peak placebo-adjusted reduction: about 5 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ), effective filtration fraction (peak reduction about 1.5%), and proteinuria (about 300 μg/min) were observed only during dietary sodium restriction and not during habitual sodium intake. Conclusions Dietary sodium restriction enhances the short-term kidney efficacy of selective endothelin-A receptor antagonism in proteinuric CKD while preserving its beneficial systemic hemodynamic effects. As ERAs become established therapies for proteinuric kidney disease, these findings suggest that adherence to dietary sodium restriction may maximize their kidney-protective benefits. Whether the acute changes demonstrated here translate into long-term kidney protection requires prospective evaluation.

items.title: Examining blood-based biological correlates of cognition and intra-individual variability in bipolar disorder; an exploratory analysis.
items.abstract: Background Cognitive impairment is a common and functionally meaningful characteristic of bipolar disorder (BD), but its biological underpinnings are yet to be fully established. Emerging evidence posits telomere length and peripheral inflammation as prospective factors of interest. We explored the independent and combined associations between these biological factors and cognition in BD. Methods One hundred and forty-nine participants (n = 92 people with BD and n = 57 healthy controls) completed cognitive assessments of processing speed, sustained attention, working memory, executive function, and neurocognitive intraindividual variability. Whole-blood and plasma samples were provided, from which genomic DNA was extracted to measure telomere length, and several inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, of which the inflammatory which were measured in composite. Associations and moderator effects were examined using regression models with interaction terms. Results Poorer cognition, higher intraindividual variability, and shorter telomeres were found in the BD group compared to healthy controls. No significant group differences in either of the inflammatory composites were identified, and no independent associations of cognition with telomere length or either inflammatory composite were observed. However, an interaction of the biological variables was evident in the BD group, whereby BD patients with a combination of shorter telomeres and high levels of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines demonstrated poorer processing speed. Conclusion This exploratory study suggests a proof-of-concept that at least one aspect of cognition in BD may be associated with cumulative biological dysregulation, given preliminary findings that poor processing speed is associated with the combined, rather than the isolated effects, of telomere length and inflammation.

items.title: Synaptic injury and neurodegeneration: recent advances in mechanisms of SGN injury in ARHL.
items.abstract: Age-related hearing loss (ARHL) is a common chronic sensory disorder among the elderly. It causes communication difficulties and is closely associated with cognitive decline and depression. The degeneration of cochlear spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs) and early damage to ribbon synapses are crucial processes in ARHL. Since synaptic dysfunction often occurs before hair cell loss and threshold elevations, it contributes to hidden hearing loss and adversely affects the efficacy of cochlear implantation. However, the mechanisms by which synaptic injury drives SGN aging are not yet fully understood. This review systematically overviews the degeneration of ribbon synapses and SGN in ARHL, including the molecular and functional heterogeneity of SGN subtypes, the spatial and temporal patterns of ribbon synapses, the pathological mechanisms and the cell death pathways of SGN damage during aging. This review also identifies future research directions and emphasizes early intervention targets in ARHL, aiming to provide a systematic theoretical framework for the early prevention and clinical management of ARHL.

items.title: Right-to-left shunt burden and altered white matter functional networks in stroke-free patients with patent foramen ovale.
items.abstract: Resting-state functional MRI (rsfMRI) is a useful technique for investigating the functional organization of human brain networks. Nevertheless, most rsfMRI studies in patent foramen ovale (PFO) have focused on gray-matter connectivity or structural imaging, whereas white-matter functional networks remain poorly characterized. PFO has been hypothesized to expose the brain to recurrent right-to-left shunt (RLS)-related microembolic, vasoactive and hemodynamic stressors, but whether these stressors are associated with altered white-matter functional organization in patients without overt stroke is unclear. The current study used rsfMRI to evaluate white-matter functional networks in stroke-free PFO patients and healthy controls. In the PFO group, RLS severity and anatomical features were characterized using contrast-enhanced transcranial Doppler and transesophageal echocardiography. Nine large-scale white-matter networks were identified by K-means clustering of voxel-wise white-matter functional connectivity. Evaluation of spontaneous oscillations and inter-network functional connectivity showed that PFO patients had widespread reductions in fast Fourier transform-derived band-averaged amplitude, mainly involving motor, occipital, cerebellar, deep and cingulum networks, and consistently reduced inferior frontal-to-fronto-temporal connectivity across frequency bands. Higher RLS grade was associated with lower white-matter amplitude in several networks, whereas PFO anatomical measurements showed no independent associations after multiple-comparison correction. Exploratory mediation analyses showed no significant indirect pathways after FDR correction. In this cross-sectional study, these findings suggest that RLS burden may be relevant to subclinical white-matter functional vulnerability in stroke-free PFO.

items.title: Where could the brain keep a symbol?
items.abstract: Neuroscience routinely describes memories as stored neural symbols, yet durable memory and successful retrieval do not establish a separately accessible symbolic vehicle. I distinguish retention, the claim that a physical change persists and later influences behavior, from symbolic storage, the stronger computational claim that a description can be accessed independently of the operation it specifies. The criterion is functional and system-relative and does not rule out neural activity as access. It requires specifying, before testing, the candidate vehicle, its proposed use, the system boundary, and an endogenous route reaching the vehicle without using it. DNA meets the criterion: replication preserves nucleotide sequence without producing the encoded gene product. Evidence from synapses and circuits establishes persistent, functionally useful organization but has not shown this separation for any neural memory vehicle; in these states, identified reads are executions that modify what they read. Hippocampal replay, neuromodulation, and artificial-network checkpoints show that the verdict depends on the vehicle and operations compared. I agree with Gallistel that intracellular nucleic acid mechanisms could provide a genuine store, but disagree that behavioral precision alone requires one. Maintained coupling, in which memory is sustained by continual recalibration rather than read from a store, offers an alternative whose predictions depend on error source: drift can be corrected where a reference signal remains, but a unique, never-revisited episode offers none. Current evidence favors retention without symbolic storage in synapses and circuits; I propose operational tests that could overturn this verdict. Either way, retention and use remain memory.

items.title: Mismatch Negativity and General Cognitive Ability - A Meta-Analysis.
items.abstract: Intelligence or general cognitive ability (GCA) is fundamental to human behavior and cognition. It impacts important life outcomes like educational success, and even health and longevity have been related to differences in GCA. Understanding the biological basis of such individual variations presents a crucial goal of neuroscience. The mismatch negativity (MMN) is an event-related brain potential that can be measured when-within a series of frequent standard stimuli, rare deviants are presented-and is suggested to reflect conscious (active) or unconscious (passive) detection processes of the brain. Importantly, variations in MMN amplitude and latency have been linked to differences in GCA. Yet findings vary considerably. This preregistered meta-analysis provides a comprehensive and structured overview of the current state of research. Following the study selection process in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines, and the rating of study design quality with the Study Design and Implementation Assessment Device for Individual Difference Research (DIAD-ID), the association between GCA and MMN amplitude and latency was examined in 645 healthy adults across 12 included studies. The estimated across-sample associations between MMN and GCA were small, but significant (MMN amplitude-GCA: r = -0.09, MMN latency-GCA: r = -0.16; p < 0.01) and moderators were identified. Between-sample heterogeneity was moderate, with no evidence of publication bias. Our findings suggest that higher cognitive ability is associated with slightly stronger and faster MMN responses. However, the low estimated across-sample effect sizes and the small number of included studies also highlight the need for more research.

items.title: Prediction of surgical outcome using cyclic spectral coherent networks of intracranial EEG signals.
items.abstract: Epilepsy is a network disorder characterized by abnormal brain connectivity. Identifying network-level biomarkers is critical for improving surgical outcome prediction and understanding seizure dynamics. This study proposes a novel framework to assess the brain network organization of epileptic patients using cyclostationary-based connectivity matrices derived from intracranial EEG (iEEG) signals. The iEEG recordings of epileptic patients with surgical outcomes classified as Engel I (n=19) and Engel II+ (n=19) groups are considered for this study. Cyclic Spectral Coherence (CSC) based connectivity matrices are estimated from the preictal, ictal and postictal seizure phases using Welch's method. Further, network hubs are identified using centrality measures and the Resection Hub Alignment Degree (RHAD) metric is computed to quantify the alignment between the hubs and surgically resected nodes. The results of the cyclostationary spectrum reveal non-zero spectral correlation density, confirming the presence of rhythmic patterns in iEEG signals with dominant peaks observed in the SOZ regions. Furthermore, preictal RHAD-EVC differentiates the seizure-free and non-seizure-free patient groups (p < 0.01) and achieves an AUC of 0.64 for postoperative surgical outcome prediction. The results of the proposed method are in good agreement with those reported in previous studies. Overall, the cyclic spectral coherent network-based RHAD metric may serve as a robust index that captures the network disruptions beyond geometric overlap. The proposed framework demonstrates potential to serve as an ancillary tool for characterizing network alterations rather than as a standalone predictive indicator.

items.title: Single cell RNA-Seq in crim1<sup>-/-</sup> eyes in zebrafish shows dysregulation of β-actin and genes involved in cell adhesion and motility.
items.abstract: Purpose Cysteine-Rich Motor Neuron Protein 1 (CRIM1) haploinsufficiency is associated with eye defects, including coloboma, in humans. We previously generated a zebrafish model of reduced crim1 function that had smaller and malformed lenses and an abnormal retinal ganglion cell (RGC) layer, but our understanding of the gene dysregulation causing these ocular findings is limited. Methods To address this knowledge gap, we performed scRNA-Seq in dissected eyes from the crim1 -/- mutants and controls at 48 hours post fertilization and focused our analysis on cell types with differential expression of crim1. We used Comprehensive Multi-omics Platform for Biological InterpretatiOn (CompBio) to identify enriched biological themes. Results We identified a 31-cluster model that provided clear separation of ocular cell types and tissues. Lectin, galactoside-binding, soluble (lgals2b), orthologous to LGALS2 that was shown to bind β 1 -integrin in T cells, was the most upregulated gene in the Lens cluster. We found significant downregulation of integrin 1b.1 (itgb1b.1) and integrin 1b.2 (itgb1b.2) in the Corneal cluster of the crim1 -/- mutants. In the RGC clusters, serpin family E member 3 (serpine3) that is associated with retinal layering and sidekick cell adhesion molecule 1b (sdk1b) that encodes a protein involved in cell adhesion were upregulated, whereas glycoprotein M6A (gpm6a) was downregulated. CompBio identified numerous themes, including actin cytoskeleton remodeling, Wnt signaling, apoptosis and cell cycle regulation, and extracellular matrix organization. We found that β-actin expression was absent from the outer plexiform layer of the crim1 -/- mutants. Conclusions Our results support the known function of crim1 in integrin binding, cell adhesion, and apoptosis, but also uncover novel differentially expressed genes, including β-actin, lgals2b, serpine3, sdk1b, and gpm6a.

items.title: Modulation of acute pain by interactions between orexin 1 and opioid receptors in the hippocampal dentate gyrus: Insights from the tail-flick test in male rats.
items.abstract: Emerging evidence implicates the hippocampal dentate gyrus (DG) in the modulation of nociceptive processing. However, the interaction between orexinergic and opioidergic signaling within this region remains unclear. The present study investigated the functional interplay between the orexin 1 receptor (OX1R) and the opioid receptors in the DG region in the regulation of acute pain. Adult male Wistar rats received unilateral intra-DG microinjections, and nociceptive thresholds were assessed using the tail-flick test. Behavioral data demonstrated that morphine (10 and 25mmol) produced a significant increase in tail-flick latency, which was attenuated by pretreatment with the opioid receptor antagonist naloxone (15 and 45mmol). Likewise, intra-DG administration of orexin-A (OXA; 0.5, 1, and 2 nmol) significantly elevated nociceptive thresholds, and this effect was reduced by the selective OX1R antagonist SB334867 (10, 30, and 100 nmol), confirming the involvement of OX1R signaling. Naloxone was administered before OXA, and SB334867 was administered before morphine to assess pharmacological cross-antagonism. Blockade of opioid receptors significantly diminished OXA-induced antinociception, whereas OX1R antagonism attenuated morphine-induced analgesia, a pattern consistent with mutual cross-modulation between these systems. Total distance traveled in the open field did not differ among groups at the maximum single-agent doses. Collectively, these findings are compatible with a functional interaction between OX1R and opioid receptors within the DG area in acute pain modulation and indicate that orexinergic signaling contributes to acute antinociceptive processing. Whether targeting this pathway can modulate opioid efficacy, or affect opioid-related adverse effects, was not tested.

items.title: Nicotine increases dopamine signaling in the nucleus accumbens in male Wistar rats.
items.abstract: Nicotine is the primary tobacco alkaloid that reinforces tobacco use. Increase in extracellular dopamine levels within the nucleus accumbens (NAc) is believed to mediate the reinforcing effects of nicotine. Historically, microdialysis and in vivo voltammetry have been commonly used to monitor nicotine-induced dopamine increase with different temporal resolution and dopamine specificity. Fiber photometry coupled with GPCR-based dopamine sensors recently emerged as a versatile tool for monitoring dopamine signaling linked to drug and drug-related behaviors at a subsecond time scale and with high dopamine specificity. Studies with this technique have begun to uncover rapid dopamine dynamics induced by nicotine aerosol exposure and subcutaneous injection. Intravenous self-administration (IVSA) remains a commonly used behavioral assay for assessing the reinforcing effects of nicotine. However, dopamine dynamics associated with nicotine IVSA remains to be determined. The current study investigated nicotine effects on rapid dopamine dynamics in the NAc following both passive and volitional IV nicotine administration and pharmacological regulation of these effects by nicotine-related compounds. Passive IV infusion of nicotine at 0.06 mg/kg significantly enhanced rapid dopamine signaling in the NAc and such effects were abolished by pretreatment with mecamylamine, varenicline, or bupropion. Volitional nicotine IVSA at 0.06 mg/kg/infusion also increased dopamine signaling in the NAc that was time-locked to active lever press and cue light presentation for nicotine infusion. These results suggest that increase in rapid dopamine signaling in the NAc may underlie the effects of nicotine and that inhibition of such effects may contribute to the pharmacological effects of nicotine-related compounds.

items.title: Baseline diffusion MRI markers of interstitial fluid dynamics are associated with subsequent amyloid conversion in cognitively normal individuals.
items.abstract: Background Emerging evidence suggests that early disruption of interstitial fluid (ISF) dynamics may precede amyloid-β (Aβ) deposition, and diffusion MRI-derived indices offer noninvasive markers of ISF properties. We investigated whether baseline ISF-sensitive diffusion MRI markers differ between Aβ-negative (-) cognitively normal (CN) individuals who subsequently convert to Aβ-positivity and those who remain Aβ (-), and whether these markers are associated with subsequent Aβ accumulation. Methods We included Aβ (-) CN participants from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative cohorts who had baseline MRI and longitudinal amyloid PET. Based on longitudinal amyloid PET standardized uptake value ratio (SUVR), participants were classified as 18 converters who exceeded the Aβ-positivity threshold at least once during follow-up and 16 non-converters who remained Aβ (-) throughout follow-up. Baseline diffusion MRI-derived ISF markers, cortical free water (FW), the diffusion tensor image analysis along the perivascular space (ALPS) index corrected for white-matter microstructural asymmetry (corrected ALPS index), and perivascular space volume fraction, were compared between groups, together with baseline Aβ, tau, and neurodegeneration biomarkers. Associations between baseline MRI measures and annualized change in amyloid PET SUVR were also assessed. Results Converters showed higher cortical FW and lower corrected ALPS index than non-converters, despite no baseline group differences in Aβ, tau, or neurodegeneration markers. Among converters, higher baseline FW was associated with a faster annualized increase in amyloid PET SUVR. Conclusions Our findings indicate that baseline diffusion MRI markers of ISF dynamics are associated with subsequent Aβ-positivity conversion and Aβ accumulation in initially Aβ (-) CN individuals, suggesting that alterations in ISF dynamics may be detectable before overt Aβ deposition.

items.title: Genetic Variants and Domain-Specific Cognitive Function in the Alzheimer's Disease Continuum: A Systematic Review.
items.abstract: Background APOE ε4 is the strongest common genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease and is associated with age-related cognitive decline. Whether its association with cognition, and that of other candidate variants, is uniform across cognitive domains or domain-specific remains unclear. Objective To synthesize single-variant candidate-gene evidence on domain-specific cognitive function (episodic memory, executive function, language, visuospatial function, attention, processing speed) in the Alzheimer's disease-indexed literature, beyond APOE alone. Methods We searched PubMed, Embase, and Scopus on 18 June 2026 without date restriction (PRISMA 2020; PROSPERO CRD420261446003). Of 6,453 records, we included 111 studies; all search strings required an Alzheimer's disease term. We applied two risk-of-bias tools to every study. Two reviewers extracted and appraised data using AI assistance and verified them against the source text, without reporting agreement statistics. Synthesis was narrative by domain, with an exploratory effect-size meta-analysis for APOE. Results APOE was examined in 70 of 111 studies (63%), and 30 further genes were examined in two or more studies each. Detrimental APOE associations were most consistent for episodic memory (48 of 75 findings; sign test p=3.3×10⁻⁹) and executive function (28 of 54; p=5.1×10⁻⁴). The direction of association did not differ between domains (χ²(5)=2.13, p=0.83; 84% detrimental), but detection frequency did (null results 28% to 65%; χ²(5)=20.16, p=0.001). In an exploratory meta-analysis of 36 studies, pooled ε4 effects on performance were small and negative in all six domains, significantly so only for episodic memory (Hedges' g=-0.14, 95% CI -0.21 to -0.07; executive function -0.07, -0.13 to 0.00), and within the same studies the episodic memory effect exceeded the executive function and language effects. The episodic memory result was robust to square-root sample-size weighting, age restriction and significance-threshold re-analysis; the executive function result was less robust, and the two risk-of-bias tools disagreed on whether either survives quality stratification. Conclusions The direction of APOE's association with cognition appears uniform across domains; it is detected most often on episodic memory measures, where its standardized effect also exceeds that on executive function and language measures, and part of the between-domain variation in detection, and possibly in effect size, may reflect the instruments used. Evidence beyond APOE is fragmented, with 93 of 123 non-APOE genes (76%) supported by a single study. Single-variant evidence from the Alzheimer's disease literature thus converges on APOE, with only preliminary evidence for a few other Alzheimer's disease risk loci, in contrast to the highly polygenic architecture that genome-wide studies describe for general cognitive function.

items.title: Examining the appeal of cigarette filters: An online randomised experiment among adults in Great Britain.
items.abstract: Cigarette filters are present in almost all cigarettes sold globally, despite providing no health protection and contributing substantially to environmental pollution. Filters may also increase cigarette appeal and reinforce misperceptions of reduced harm. This study aimed to examine the impact of cigarette filters on cigarette appeal and perceptions of health and environmental harms among adults in Great Britain. Online between-subject randomised experiment embedded within a nationally representative survey. Great Britain, May 2026. Adults aged 18 + years, recruited through the YouGov Social Omnibus survey (n = 3961). Subgroup analyses were conducted among people who currently smoked (n = 499) and people who smoked daily (n = 270). Participants were randomised to view images of cigarettes either without filters (intervention) or with filters (conventional cigarettes; comparator). The primary outcome was selecting one of the displayed cigarettes to smoke vs. selecting none. Secondary outcomes were perceptions that the cigarette was extremely harmful to health and extremely harmful to the environment. Logistic regression models were used, adjusting for age, gender and smoking status. There was strong evidence to suggest that all participants who viewed cigarettes without filters had markedly lower odds of choosing a cigarette to smoke than those who viewed cigarettes with filters [19.1% vs. 28.1%; adjusted odds ratio (AOR) = 0.46, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 0.38-0.55, P < 0.001]. Cigarettes without filters also had higher odds of being perceived as extremely harmful to health (65.2% vs. 59.9%; AOR = 1.26, 95% CI = 1.10-1.45, P = 0.001). Evidence was insufficient to conclude a difference between conditions in perceiving cigarettes as extremely harmful to the environment (41.8% vs. 44.3%; AOR = 0.89, 95% CI = 0.78-1.01, P = 0.074). Findings were similar among people who currently smoke, with participants who viewed cigarettes without (vs. with) filters having markedly lower odds of choosing a cigarette (67.4% vs. 94.2%; AOR = 0.12, 95% CI = 0.06-0.22, P < 0.001). These findings were also similar among people who smoke daily (70.7% vs. 94.8%; AOR = 0.14, 95% CI = 0.06-0.36, P < 0.001). However, evidence was insufficient to conclude differences in perceived health harms between conditions among people who smoke currently (29.8% vs. 27.8%; AOR = 1.12, 95% CI = 0.75-1.67, P = 0.588) or daily (32.2% vs. 28.6%; AOR = 0.76, 95% CI = 0.44-1.32, P = 0.324). Among adults in Great Britain viewing images of cigarettes with and without filters, cigarettes without filters were chosen less often and perceived as more harmful to health than cigarettes with filters. Given that cigarette filters provide no health protection and contribute to environmental pollution, policies that regulate or prohibit filters may support public health and environmental goals.

items.title: The neural mechanisms of fast versus slow decision-making.
items.abstract: One hallmark of intelligent behavior is the ability to optimize how much time is devoted to decisions. Yet the principles governing decision timing remain unclear. Here, we developed a novel paradigm for directly comparing decision-making between mice and humans. This approach allowed us to combine widefield and 2-photon imaging in the mouse frontal cortex with optogenetic inhibition to examine the underlying mechanisms. We found that history-dependent refinement of sequences in the medial frontal cortex (MFC), versus a thresholding mechanism in the lateral frontal cortex (LFC), provides a unified logic for decision strategy on a trial-by-trial basis. Notably, behavioral performance and strategy were profoundly disrupted by optogenetic inhibition of the MFC compared with that of the LFC, revealing a dominant cognitive role for MFC in decision selection and timing. These dynamics reflect reinforcement-learning updates that explain timing variability better than sensory evidence. Our findings provide a computational framework that unifies voluntary decision-making across species.

items.title: Clock misalignment, not structural loss, underlies memory impairment following disruption of the mushroom body.
items.abstract: The Drosophila mushroom body (MB) is a central circuit for many forms of associative learning, including olfactory conditioning, courtship conditioning, and aversive phototaxic suppression (APS). Kenyon cells (KCs), the intrinsic neurons of the MB, can be severely disrupted but not entirely eliminated by hydroxy urea (HU) treatment during development. Here, we show that HU-treated flies are profoundly impaired in short- and long-term memory under baseline conditions and that enhanced sleep restores learning in these animals. We establish the robustness of this finding using multiple behavioral assays and two independent methods to enhance sleep. Mechanistic analyses reveal that HU treatment disrupts circadian clock output, mistiming activity in γ-lobe-projecting dopaminergic neurons (DANs) and MB output neurons (MBONs). We further show that this mistiming is mediated, in part, by pigment-dispersing factor (PDF) signaling onto γ2-projecting DANs. Enhanced sleep restores the proper temporal coordination of these circuits. Strikingly, selectively reducing PDF receptor (Pdfr) signaling in these DANs also restored memory in HU-treated flies despite markedly reduced sleep, demonstrating that correcting mistimed clock signals can reproduce the restorative effects of sleep. These findings indicate that memory impairments after HU treatment can arise from disrupted temporal coordination within the MB circuit and demonstrate that downstream MBON-DAN interactions can support learning when properly regulated.

items.title: Genome writing reveals SVA retrotransposon consequences in X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism.
items.abstract: Human retrotransposon insertions are often associated with diseases. Regarding neurodegenerative X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (XDP), a human-specific SINE-VNTR-Alu (SVA) subfamily F retrotransposon was inserted in intron 32 of the TAF1 gene. Here, we genomically rewrote a portion of the mouse Taf1 allele with the corresponding 78-kb XDP patient-derived TAF1 allele. In mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs), the presence of the intronic SVA-rather than the hybrid gene structure-reduces hyTAF1 (hybrid TAF1 mRNA) levels. This leads to transcriptional downregulation of genes with TATA boxes enriched in their promoters and triggers apoptosis. Chromatin and transcriptome profiling revealed that intronic SVAs are actively transcribed, forming barriers that likely impede transcription elongation. In mice, neuronal-lineage TAF1 humanization resulted in lethality in male progeny within 2 months. XDP male mice developed severe atrophy centered on the striatum-the same brain region affected in XDP patients. Lastly, CRISPRa-mediated activation of hyTAF1 restored mESC viability, suggesting that boosting TAF1 transcription could be a therapeutic approach.

items.title: Myelin pathology is a key feature of X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism.
items.abstract: X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (XDP) is an adult-onset movement disorder predominantly affecting males of Filipino descent. It is caused by the insertion of a SINE-variable number of tandem repeat (VNTR)-Alu subfamily F (SVA_F) retrotransposon in the TATA-box binding protein-associated factor 1 (TAF1) gene. A barrier to XDP research has been the lack of animal models. Here, we introduce a conditional humanized XDP mouse model harboring a hybrid mouse-human Taf1/TAF1 gene (hyTAF1) containing the pathogenic SVA_F. We activated hyTAF1 in Nestin+ cells and found the resulting XDP male mice recapitulate features of human XDP, including severe motor impairment and striatal atrophy. Transcriptomic, histological, and electron microscopy analyses revealed a reduction in oligodendrocyte-lineage cells and myelin disruption. Consistent with this, postmortem brain tissue from XDP patients revealed similar myelin pathology, including loss of myelin in the medial prefrontal cortex. These results identify oligodendrocyte dysfunction and myelin loss as major contributors to XDP, providing new mechanistic insight into this disorder.

items.title: CD19 CAR T cell therapy alters disease-associated immune signatures in multiple sclerosis.
items.abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic inflammatory central nervous system (CNS) disease. Although current immunotherapies control relapses, they have limited impact on progression, which might reflect incomplete access to or modulation of compartmentalized CNS inflammation. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells can infiltrate tissues, but their ability to access and eliminate immune cells residing in the CNS remains elusive. We report the treatment of five individuals with progressive or relapsing-remitting MS with autologous CD19 CAR T cells to assess safety-relevant aspects, CNS bioavailability, and compartment-specific effects. The intervention induces remodeling of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) B cell pool, with a sustained reduction in CSF humoral biomarkers. Notably, CSF-infiltrating CAR T cells selectively upregulate phosphodiesterase 7B, while reconstituted peripheral B cells show altered cytokine and homing profiles. These findings indicate compartment-specific immunomodulation beyond peripheral B cell depletion and support controlled trials to test safety, durability, and efficacy.

items.title: Sir Roger Bannister (1929-2018): beyond the track, documenting his influence in the field of autonomic neurology.
items.abstract: Sir Roger Bannister, best known for running the sub-four-minute mile, was influential in establishing the field of autonomic neurology. His early experiences studying exercise physiology, spinal cord injury, and thermoregulation shaped his interest in the mechanisms underlying autonomic regulation. The development of therapeutic approaches such as droxidopa to treat dopamine beta-hydroxylase deficiency could not have been accomplished without Bannister's dedication and contributions. Through his research, collaborations, and leadership in establishing the Clinical Autonomic Research Society, Bannister helped transform a field that was once dismissed as 'no more than an overture' into a lasting discipline in the field of neurology.

items.title: Postsurgical seizure occurrence and cognitive outcome between temporal and non-temporal lobe epilepsy: MRI-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy for drug-resistant epilepsy.
items.abstract: MRI-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy (MRgLITT) is a novel minimally invasive intervention for drug-resistant epilepsy. We assess the surgical outcome and cognitive outcome of MRgLITT for temporal and non-temporal epilepsy. 27 patients with refractory epilepsy scheduled for MRgLITT from 2023 to 2024 at the First Affiliated Hospital of Fujian Medical University were enrolled. Epileptogenic zones were located with non-invasive evaluation system ± stereoelectroencephalography (sEEG). The Chinese version of the Western Aphasia Battery (WAB), the Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test (AVLT), Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) were performed to assess cognitive function. Demographic data, surgical and cognitive outcome were compared between temporal and non-temporal lobe epilepsy. 10 patients had temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE), all involving mesial temporal targets, and 17 patients had non-temporal lobe epilepsy (nTLE). All patients were followed up for seizure occurrence after surgery. 18 patients completed MMSE, 12 patients completed WAB and AVLT. The number of patients achieved favourable outcome (Engel Class I or ILAE Class 1-2) was more in TLE patients: Engel Class I in 9/10 vs. 5/17, P = 0.004; ILAE Class 1-2 in 8/10 vs. 6/17, P = 0.046. Postoperative cognitive decline was more common in TLE patients, including WAB decline (3/5 vs. 0/7, P = 0.045), AVLT‑immediate recall decline (3/5 vs. 0/7, P = 0.045), and MMSE changes (2 improved, 1 declined in TLE vs. no change in nTLE, P = 0.043). Patients with TLE achieved better seizure control than those with nTLE, whereas cognitive decline was observed mainly in TLE patients after MRgLITT. These preliminary findings suggest that MRgLITT could be an effective option for well-localized TLE, and a reasonable alternative for nTLE patients with relatively stable preservation of cognitive function.

items.title: Can negative tests rule out shunt benefit in idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus? An umbrella review of decision validity.
items.abstract: Negative pre-shunt tests may deny patients with idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH) a beneficial operation, yet their rule-out value and response-outcome validity remain uncertain. We searched six databases to 3 August 2026 for systematic reviews of pre-shunt predictors or response measurement in iNPH. Two reviewers independently selected reports and applied ROBIS; extraction was independently checked. An outcome-blind hierarchy selected one estimate per clinically matched question; reviews were not re-pooled. Paired accuracy was translated into illustrative, non-causal probabilities across prespecified pretest scenarios. The review was retrospectively registered (PROSPERO CRD420261494316). Forty-one reviews yielded 192 findings, 155 estimates and 139 response definitions. Thirty-two had high ROBIS risk; 14/15 AMSTAR 2-applicable reviews had critically low confidence. Author-defined rules accounted for 92/139 definitions, 134/139 omitted a minimum clinically important difference and none documented a threshold validated for patient-important iNPH shunt response. Across 50 %, 65 % and 80 % pretest scenarios, several negative results left substantial modeled response probability. At 65 %, six of seven estimates left 47.9-60.2 %; extended drainage was 11.6 % but had a wide plausible range. Ten of 11 clinical cells depended on one anchor review. Current review-level evidence does not establish any single negative test, absent imaging sign, biomarker or comorbidity as a validated stand-alone exclusion rule for shunting. Multimodal probability updating and validated domain-specific outcomes are priorities.

items.title: Deictic Gestures and Developmental Skills in Down Syndrome: The Role of Hand Points.
items.abstract: This study aimed to characterize deictic gesture form and communicative intent in children with Down syndrome (DS) and address a clinically important limitation in how pointing is defined in assessment. Building on our prior work linking caregiver-reported total gesture use to language, motor, and pragmatic/social skills in toddlers with DS, we examined microcoded deictic gestures during naturalistic parent-child interactions, distinguishing hand points (multifinger or whole-hand points) from index-finger points and exploring associations with adaptive developmental skills. Participants were 41 children with DS (range: 36.3-88.8 months, M = 54.1 months) who completed a baseline 10-min remote in-home parent-child interaction. Gestures were coded for type, deictic form (reach, give, show, hand point, index-finger point), and communicative intent (behavioral request, joint attention). Rates were compared using Friedman tests (false discovery rate [FDR] corrected). Partial Spearman correlations examined associations between the three most frequent deictic forms (hand point, show, and give) and Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales-Third Edition (Vineland-3) growth scale values across communication, motor, and interpersonal domains, controlling for chronological age with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR (BH-FDR) correction. Children produced higher rates of deictic than nondeictic gestures. Most gestures were spontaneous, and many co-occurred with speech. Index-finger points were uncommon; hand points were more frequent and clearly referential in context (serving both requesting and joint attention functions). After age control and BH-FDR correction, hand-point rate was positively associated with Vineland-3 Interpersonal Relationships. Hand points were common, spontaneous, and communicatively meaningful in children with DS but may be overlooked when pointing is defined solely as an index-finger gesture. Measurement frameworks that credit functionally effective hand points may provide a more accurate representation of children's referential communication and inform clinical interpretation and intervention planning.

items.title: Differential Impacts of Acoustic Challenge on Three Language-Related Event-Related Brain Potential Components During Speech Processing: Evidence From the N400, the P600, and a Late Frontal Response.
items.abstract: When listening to acoustically challenging speech, listeners may strategically shift neural resources across multiple language-related cognitive processes in order to compensate for the additional demands. In the current study, we examined the impact of acoustic challenge (via speech-shaped background noise) on three language-related event-related brain potentials (ERPs): the N400 and two late positivities following the N400-a posterior P600 to syntactic violations and a late frontal effect sensitive to word expectancy. Young, normal-hearing adults (N = 48) listened in quiet and in noise (+3 dB SNR speech-shaped stationary noise) to contextually constraining sentences that ended in an expected word, an unexpected word, or a morphosyntactic violation of the expected word, while electroencephalography data were collected. Replicating prior work, we showed that an N400 expectancy effect was both reduced in amplitude and delayed in onset latency in noise. Providing novel insights into late ERP components, we found that a P600 syntax effect was reduced in amplitude by the presence of background noise. We additionally observed that the P600 response was only present for trials in which the listener successfully identified syntactic violations (irrespective of noise). In contrast to the reductions in the N400 and P600, the late frontal response was not reduced in noise. Collectively, this suggests that, while semantic retrieval and syntactic integration may be impaired by acoustic challenge, young, normal-hearing listeners may still prioritize neural resources toward prediction-related processes to help compensate for increased perceptual demands.

items.title: A "Basin of Attraction" Theory of Speech Initiation and Stuttering.
items.abstract: Recent work in motor neuroscience suggests that well-learned actions are implemented as stable, stereotyped trajectories in neural state space. The purpose of this article was to propose a theory of the neural basis of speech initiation that extends this idea to speech production and identifies a specific disruption that may underlie speech dysfluencies in stuttering. We advance a conceptual framework in which the motor program for a familiar word corresponds to a stable neural trajectory with an associated basin of attraction. We integrate findings from primate motor control, human speech neuroscience, and basal ganglia physiology to specify the role of the cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical (BGTC) circuit in initiating these trajectories. We propose that fluent speech depends on the ability of the BGTC circuit to steer the distributed speech motor network into the basin of attraction of the upcoming word's motor program. Stuttering arises when this process is unreliable or poorly coordinated, preventing the motor program from being executed until the neural state is corrected or the effective basin of attraction is broadened through compensatory mechanisms. The basin of attraction framework provides a mechanistic description of the proximal neural processes responsible for stuttering events that can account for a wide range of behavioral and neurophysiological findings in stuttering. It also aligns stuttering theory with contemporary dynamical systems approaches to motor control and generates testable predictions for future neurophysiological and neuroimaging studies.

items.title: Efficacy and Safety of 2 Rimegepant Dosing Regimens for the Prevention of Episodic Migraine: A Randomized Controlled Study.
items.abstract: Traditional preventive treatments for migraine have limitations (e.g., efficacy, adverse events [AEs], contraindications, and interactions). The aim of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of 2 rimegepant dosing regimens relative to placebo as preventive treatment for episodic migraine. This was a phase 4, randomized, placebo-controlled study. Adults with a ≥1-year history of episodic migraine (with or without aura) and 4-14 migraine attacks/month were enrolled from outpatient/research sites in 10 countries. After a 28-day observation phase, participants were randomly assigned to placebo once daily, rimegepant 75 mg every other day/alternating placebo, or rimegepant 75 mg once daily for 12-weeks of double-blind treatment. The primary end point was mean reduction from the observation phase in monthly migraine days over the entire 12-week double-blind phase analyzed using linear mixed effects modeling. Hierarchical testing was used for key secondary end points to control type I error. Safety assessments included AEs. Participants (n = 692; median age 44.0 years, 86.7% female) were treated double blind with rimegepant every other day (n = 232), rimegepant once daily (n = 229), or placebo (n = 231). The primary end point was met for both rimegepant dosing regimens, with significantly greater reductions from the observation phase in monthly migraine days over the entire double-blind phase vs placebo (least squares mean change difference [97.5% CI]) for rimegepant every other day (-0.6 [-1.22 to -0.01], p = 0.0220) and rimegepant once daily (-1.8 [-2.35 to -1.19], p < 0.0001). All 5 key secondary end points were significant vs placebo for rimegepant once daily (p < 0.0001), while for rimegepant every other day, the first key secondary end point in the hierarchy was not significant vs placebo. Most AEs were mild or moderate. Both rimegepant dosing regimens were superior to placebo for the preventive treatment of migraine and were well tolerated. This study demonstrates the efficacy and safety of rimegepant 75 mg QD in a double-blind study. The study was not designed to directly compare the rimegepant EOD and QD dosing regimens. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05217927 (clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05217927); registered January 20, 2022; first enrollment March 4, 2022. This study provides Class I evidence that in adults with more than 1-year history of episodic migraine and 4-14 migraine attacks/month, both rimegepant 75 mg every other day and rimegepant 75 mg daily were superior to placebo in reducing monthly migraine days up to 12 weeks of follow-up.
