items.title: Thermodynamics of gas giants accreting via shocks: the role of molecular hydrogen dissociation
items.abstract: Within the core-accretion framework, gas giants acquire most of their mass through accretion shocks during runaway gas accretion. The shock thermodynamics---governed by radiative cooling, accretion history, and equation of state (EoS)---sets the post-shock gas entropy and initial thermal state, strongly influencing both observables and subsequent evolution. We aim to build a coupled evolutionary model predicting the initial thermodynamic conditions, intrinsic luminosities, and upper limits on magnetic field strengths of gas giants across diverse accretion histories. We couple radiation hydrodynamics and $\mathrm{H_2}$ dissociation to long-term planetary interior evolution by training a physics-informed neural network (PINN) predictor on 1000 first-principles simulations resolving the shock physics. This PINN provides post-shock outer boundary conditions for MESA to evolve the planetary envelope beyond runaway accretion. The PINN predicts higher post-shock temperatures than the canonical cold-start model, with the discrepancy widening with planetary mass, while post-shock entropy jumps sharply when $\mathrm{H_2}$ dissociates at $\sim 2000$ K. Gas giants evolved with PINN-derived boundary conditions achieve intrinsic luminosities 4--10 times higher than cold-start models. Under optimistic assumptions, the maximum magnetic field strength at $2 R_{\mathrm{J}}$ reaches a few gauss for a $0.3 M_{\mathrm{J}}$ planet, $\sim 100$ G for $1 M_{\mathrm{J}}$, and $\sim 500$ G for $3 M_{\mathrm{J}}$. Incorporating detailed radiation hydrodynamics and realistic thermodynamics into accretion shock models yields higher initial entropies, brighter intrinsic luminosities, and stronger magnetic fields, providing improved constraints on the masses and accretion rates of directly imaged exoplanets.

items.title: Coupled sulfur cycling and bioelectrochemical regulation of lead in carbon-limited constructed wetlands: Immobilization pathways and microbial responses.
items.abstract: Constructed wetlands (CWs) are important nature-based systems for sustainable wastewater management, but simultaneous removal of lead (Pb) and conventional pollutants under low C/N conditions remains limited by electron donor deficiency and Pb-induced biological stress. This study investigated the effects of integrating microbial fuel cells (MFCs) and elemental sulfur on nutrient purification, Pb transformation, microbial responses, and bioelectricity generation in CWs planted with Iris pseudacorus. Results showed that coupling MFCs with sulfur overcame electron donor limitation under low C/N conditions, achieving removal efficiencies of 90.7%, 82.2%, and 82.7% for total phosphorus, total nitrogen, and chemical oxygen demand, respectively, and enhancing Pb removal to 87.9%. Pb was predominantly associated with the root cell wall fraction, and its extraction profile shifted toward the acetic-acid-extractable Pb fraction, consistent with restricted translocation to shoots. Microbial analyses showed that MFC and sulfur reshaped microbial community assembly and enriched functions related to carbon transformation, denitrification, sulfur cycling, and Pb immobilization. Sulfur amendment also improved bio-electrochemical performance by reducing internal resistance and increasing maximum power density. These findings indicate that integrating sulfur-driven metabolism with bioelectrochemical regulation provides a hybrid low-carbon strategy for simultaneous nutrient removal and Pb stabilization in carbon-limited wastewater treatment.

items.title: Forms of Rarity and Commonness in Boreal Bryophytes Across Contrasting Bioclimatic Landscapes.
items.abstract: Understanding how species traits and landscape conditions relate to rarity is essential for biodiversity conservation. We evaluated how forms of rarity and commonness in bryophytes are associated with life-history traits and contrasting disturbance regimes across the spruce-moss and fir-birch bioclimatic domains of eastern Canada, broad ecological regions defined by dominant forest composition, climate, and disturbance regimes. We analyzed 282 bryophyte species (~60,000 records) from 966 plots encompassing coniferous, deciduous, mixed, and open habitats. Using Rabinowitz's framework, we classified species into forms of rarity and commonness, compared richness, rarity forms, and trait composition between domains, and examined associations between rarity and life-history traits (sexual condition, asexual reproduction, and spore size) using ordination analyses. Most species were rare, predominantly habitat specialists with low local occurrence in coniferous forests and open habitats. Richness and the number of rare species were highest in the spruce-moss domain, which also harbored more species recorded exclusively within that domain. Moreover, shifts from commonness in spruce-moss to rarity in fir-birch were more frequent than the reverse, revealing asymmetric rarity patterns between domains. Dioicous species and species with large spores were more frequent among rare taxa, suggesting limited dispersal potential. Rarity patterns also closely matched disturbance regimes and landscape composition: the mixed-forest-dominated fir-birch domain supported broad-habitat species with low local occurrence, whereas old-growth coniferous stands in spruce-moss supported rare specialists. Together, these findings indicate that bryophyte rarity is strongly associated with life-history traits and landscape conditions. The spruce-moss domain sustains greater richness of rare habitat specialists, highlighting the conservation value of its extensive old-growth coniferous forests. Protecting these habitats may be critical for maintaining bryophyte diversity, particularly for species with reduced dispersal capacity. This trait-based rarity framework provides a baseline for monitoring and conserving bryophyte assemblages under landscape change.

items.title: Applying Two-Eyed Seeing to Pair Indigenous Ecological Calendars and Community Science Data for Biodiversity Monitoring in Amazonia.
items.abstract: Pairing Indigenous and Western ecological knowledge can enhance our understanding of phenological patterns, but epistemological differences, power imbalances, and histories of exclusion often limit this integration. To address these challenges, we adopted the Two-Eyed Seeing conceptual framework, which emphasizes learning from the strengths of both knowledge systems through co-developing questions, sharing knowledge mobilization, and co-producing insights. Our biocultural conservation dialogs brought together local ethnographic leaders, Indigenous scholars, and Western researchers in ecology and anthropology in Amazonia. Within the Pamiwã Indigenous territory in the Colombian Amazon, we co-developed research questions about seasonal variation in bird diversity (species richness, composition, and the relative abundance of culturally important species), as well as the effects of climate change. We documented and mobilized knowledge from both systems: Indigenous knowledge collected by Elders and apprentices during an ethno-ornithology education program was condensed into a culturally embedded ecological calendar, while data from the Western-oriented eBird community science platform (mainly contributed by avitourists) provided a second line of evidence. We compared these datasets to assess similarities and differences. Our findings revealed both convergence and divergence. Patterns in species richness and the relative abundance of culturally important birds were broadly similar, while species composition showed more variation over the year. These differences reflect distinct approaches: Indigenous observers draw on culturally embedded experience, environmental change, and resource use, whereas avitourists focus on spotting more and rarer birds. Biocultural conservation thus requires integrative, adaptive methods. Our study shows that the Two-Eyed Seeing framework can guide the pairing of Indigenous and Western knowledge systems, providing a tool for long-term biodiversity monitoring that aligns global platforms like eBird with local priorities and helps safeguard biodiversity and cultural, ancestral, and spiritual values. Iterative ecological calendars, framed by Two-Eyed Seeing, offer adaptive strategies for communities to monitor biodiversity and manage their territories.

items.title: Genetic Integrity of Selected Brown Trout Populations From Pomeranian Lake District: A Quest for Autochthony.
items.abstract: Global climate change, habitat fragmentation and widespread anthropogenic pressure pose severe threats to the genetic integrity of native salmonid populations worldwide. In particular, the pervasive practice of stocking has frequently led to the erosion of local gene pools through introgression with domesticated or non-local strains. In Poland, rivers draining the Pomeranian Lake District are among the few remaining habitats that still support indigenous brown trout populations, particularly in small sites isolated by barriers or lakes. Here, we selected eight locations harbouring potentially native populations to assess their genetic integrity. Using 13 microsatellite DNA loci, we compared the genotypes of these wild populations with those of the main hatchery strains used for stocking in Poland. Our results suggest that several populations, specifically those from small, isolated tributaries, can be considered potentially indigenous. However, the analysis also reveals that even these small tributaries have been significantly influenced by stocking with material from diverse sources. These findings highlight the urgent need for genetic monitoring and the implementation of conservation strategies focused on preserving the remaining wild genetic resources.

items.title: Multi-Scale Responses of Woody Seedlings and Saplings to Fire and Grass Removal in Indian Savannas.
items.abstract: Tropical savannas are increasingly shaped by altered fire regimes and the dominance of unpalatable grasses. Despite the global prevalence of these drivers, multi-scale experimental manipulations of both fire and native grass competition remain limited, particularly in Asian systems. We evaluated the interactive effects of short-term fire exclusion and the removal of the dominant grass Cymbopogon on woody seedling diversity and sapling growth across an Indian savanna landscape. Our results indicate that fire exclusion and grass removal are necessary to increase seedling abundance and regional (γ-scale) diversity. These responses were conditional on land-use intensity (LUI), with diversity increases observed only at lower LUI levels and broader spatial grains. Furthermore, saplings in the combined treatment exhibited significantly higher root collar diameter (RCD) growth, without evidence of an increase in herbivory or moisture stress. Long-term monitoring across varying land-use intensities is required to validate these multi-scale conservation strategies. These findings underscore that maintaining savanna biodiversity requires an integrated, scale-aware approach. Disrupting the grass-fire cycle through combined interventions and managing anthropogenic pressure is essential for the conservation of tropical savannas experiencing shifts in grass dominance and fire frequency.

items.title: Environmental Drivers of Genetic Differentiation in a Seasonally Connected Archipelago.
items.abstract: Understanding the environmental drivers of connectivity is essential for predicting species persistence in spatially structured landscapes. While the consequences of changing environmental conditions on dispersal and community assembly are well recognized, their relative importance remains poorly understood in temperate island systems. Although connectivity in marine islands is well studied, the role of seasonal filters such as ice bridges and prevailing wind patterns in temperate systems is less understood. We investigated how seasonal ice cover, snow depth, and wind patterns influence genetic connectivity in red-backed voles (Clethrionomys gapperi) across a temperate freshwater archipelago. Location: Apostle Islands, National Lakeshore, Lake Superior, USA. Time period: 2017-2022. Major taxa studied: Red-backed voles (Clethrionomys gapperi Vigors, 1830). We live-trapped and genotyped 228 C. gapperi from 17 islands and Bayfield Peninsula, WI. We estimated genetic diversity and gene flow and assessed genetic differentiation in relation to two resistance surfaces: a winter metric integrating long-term lake-ice probability and the number of days having ≥ 15 cm snow depth, and a summer metric derived from prevailing wind vectors. C. gapperi populations were genetically structured, with moderate levels of inbreeding across islands, yet exhibited evidence of gene flow throughout the archipelago. Genetic differentiation was best explained by winter resistance rather than Euclidean distance alone, whereas wind resistance had no detectable effect. Network analysis identified central islands that contributed disproportionately to overall genetic connectivity, highlighting their potential role as stepping-stones for dispersal. Winter conditions governed by ice and snow exert a stronger influence on connectivity in small-mammal populations than distance alone. As the duration and stability of ice and snow cover decline, the shortening or loss of these seasonal corridors may increase isolation in small-mammal populations. Incorporating dynamic seasonal processes into connectivity analyses is therefore essential for predicting population persistence under changing climate conditions.

items.title: Genomic Insights Into Ancestry and Genetic Structure of Wild Boar in Northern Europe.
items.abstract: The distribution and genetic structure of ungulates are shaped by a mixture of ancient and recent processes, reflecting both natural colonization and human-mediated translocations following the last glaciation and, in some cases, hybridization with domestic forms. Here, we present the first comprehensive analysis of the genetic structure of wild boar Sus scrofa (n = 101) in northern Europe, analyzed in relation to samples from continental Europe, Asia, and North Africa (755 wild boar and 273 domestic pigs, S. domesticus). We tested the consistency of historical accounts suggesting that wild boar colonized Finland from the Baltic states via Russia, whereas the Swedish and Norwegian populations originated from animals that escaped from Swedish game parks and enclosures in the 1970s, with ancestry from Germany or Central Europe. As predicted, wild boar from Finland clustered with populations from the Baltic region, whereas individuals from Sweden and Norway formed a distinct genetic cluster most closely related to wild boar from western Europe. We also corroborated historical records indicating multiple release sites in Sweden, which are reflected in southern, northwestern, and eastern genetic clusters. Wild boar that colonized Norway originated from both the eastern and northwestern Swedish clusters. Populations in Norway and Sweden exhibited relatively low genomic diversity and signatures of recent inbreeding. We detected evidence of minor introgression from domestic pigs in wild boar from Finland, Sweden, and Norway. Wild boar is a controversial species due to its high invasive potential and epidemiological importance as a reservoir for notifiable diseases such as African swine fever. We discuss how our results inform the differing management statuses (native vs. invasive) in the Fennoscandian countries. Overall, our study highlights the complex history of large mammals at the northern edge of their European distribution, shaped by an interplay of natural expansion and human-mediated translocations.

items.title: Environmentally Cued Sex Determination Evolves and Persists Under Variable Environmental Conditions.
items.abstract: Environmental sex determination (ESD), in which organisms start as one sex but may switch to a different sex during their lifetimes, is a rare but widely dispersed sexual system. The evolutionary dynamics governing this switch are, however, unknown. We investigate environmental sex determination by asking what conditions influence the evolution of the sex-change threshold in a population of species with ESD. We use a combination of theory and field data collected on multi-year populations of the sexually plastic species Acer pensylvanicum. Previous experimental research has shown that this tree species exhibits environmental sex determination, with injury and associated damage as sex-change cues for shifts from the male to female sexual phase. We found that the damage level at which a sex change occurred evolved to be lower over time, promoting an increasingly early switch to female function. Variability in local conditions affected the evolution of this damage threshold, potentially leading to different mean damage at which individuals might switch sex in different populations. Our results support the idea that, for some species, ESD is not merely a waypoint to separate sexes but a stable sexual system.

items.title: The miR-11-3p/SNF axis modulates diet-responsive plasticity in larval molt number in Bombyx mori.
items.abstract: Developmental plasticity enables insects to modify their developmental trajectories in response to environmental fluctuations. Here, we investigated diet-responsive plasticity in larval molt number, or moltinism, using the trimolter (3M) mutant SMJ (Short-instar Millet-yellow Jiangsu) of Bombyx mori. Stage-restricted feeding with old mulberry leaves increased the tetramolter (4M) proportion in SMJ and identified the second larval instar as a major period of dietary sensitivity. Transcriptomic and endocrine analyses revealed differences in cuticle formation and hormone-related processes in SMJ relative to its 4M parent MJ (Millet-yellow Jiangsu). Stage-matched endocrine profiling further showed that key events in the prothoracicotropic hormone-20-hydroxyecdysone axis and juvenile hormone-related processes occurred later in SMJ than in MJ. In SMJ, sustained hormonal perturbation during the second and third larval instars increased the 4M proportion, supporting a link between endocrine timing and moltinism plasticity. Using a robust model of calcium carbonate-induced moltinism shift, midgut small RNA sequencing identified miR-11-3p as a candidate regulator of diet-responsive plasticity in moltinism. Treatment with a miR-11-3p mimic markedly increased the 4M proportion in SMJ, whereas miR-11 knockout increased the 3M proportion in the 4M DaZao background under inductive conditions. Target prediction followed by expression and functional screening prioritized SNF (encoding U1 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein A), whose direct targeting by miR-11-3p was validated by dual-luciferase reporter assays; SNF knockdown phenocopied miR-11-3p mimic treatment by increasing the 4M proportion. Collectively, these findings identify the miR-11-3p/SNF axis as a post-transcriptional regulator that links dietary cues to plasticity in larval molt number.

items.title: From stable high costs to variable low costs: A continuum of non-breeding energy expenditure strategies in North Atlantic seabirds.
items.abstract: In the wild, many animals track shifting resource availability, a capacity with profound implications for fitness and population viability. Mobile species capable of long-distance movement can access a variety of habitats when not breeding, driving individuals to employ distinct behavioural strategies as they move through environments with contrasting effects on energetic costs (e.g. locomotion or thermoregulation) or gains (e.g. food intake). How energy expenditure is managed during this period may influence the degree to which individuals must accommodate variable resource demand, while its accumulation over time may affect how easily individuals rebuild condition ahead of reproduction. Using light-level geolocation-immersion loggers, we modelled the coefficient of variation in weekly (WEE COV_NB ; reflecting stable vs. variable energy expenditure) and total (TEE NB ) non-breeding season energy expenditure for 8 to 33 North Atlantic populations of six pelagic seabird species contrasting in movement ability and distribution. Within-species, we tested for population differences in WEE COV_NB and TEE NB , and, within-individuals, a link between the two (i.e. whether periods of above-average weekly energy expenditure, WEE, accumulate over time or are offset by periods of below-average WEE, leading to lower TEE NB ). Between-population differences in WEE COV_NB and TEE NB were strongest in diving species with high flight costs, where both metrics increased with decreasing individual encountered sea surface temperature (a driver of thermoregulatory costs) and WEE COV_NB increased with individual migratory distance (two diving species only). We further identified a continuum of energy expenditure strategies, with individuals of all species except northern fulmars spanning low TEE NB -high WEE COV_NB to high TEE NB -low WEE COV_NB . This suggests that multiple energetic pathways for navigating the non-breeding season are possible in this marine region. Ultimately, these analyses underscore energetic trade-offs shaping non-breeding season movement strategies, with implications for energy demand and fitness. As energy expenditure must be matched by intake, non-breeding seabirds in the North Atlantic likely differ in the magnitude and timing of resource requirement. These populations may thus differ in their vulnerability to stressors that further elevate costs or reduce access to prey and in their capacity to cope with environmental change.

items.title: From eDNA to food webs: AI-enabled metaweb construction for lakes which captures non-random species assemblies.
items.abstract: Food-web structure reveals ecological processes that community composition alone cannot. The rapid uptake of environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling has greatly expanded freshwater biodiversity data, creating a need for equally scalable methods to assess trophic structure, particularly in under-represented regions and among overlooked small-bodied consumers. Metawebs-regional inventories of trophic interactions used to infer local realised food webs-offer a promising solution. We developed an AI-assisted workflow to infer predator-prey interactions and used it to build a regional metaweb for New Zealand lakes from eDNA data. From a regional pool of 312 freshwater taxa, we produced a high-confidence-link (HCL) network and a broader all-consumers (AC) network. We validated the workflow against expert assessment and compared local networks from 15 lakes with null models to test for non-random structure. Observed communities had significantly higher connectance and mean trophic level than random assemblages, indicating that trophic interactions constrain community assembly. These patterns were stronger in HCL than AC networks. Food-web metrics-especially modularity-were also more sensitive to environmental gradients than species richness, providing insight beyond conventional biodiversity measures. This scalable, cost-effective framework infers trophic structure from eDNA data and can support ecosystem monitoring, management and prioritisation of lakes for targeted investigation.

items.title: Joined Up Landscapes: Embedding Nature-Based Solutions in UK Food Systems for Climate Adaptation.
items.abstract: Food and land systems in the United Kingdom face growing challenges from climate change, biodiversity loss, and ongoing uncertainty regarding transitions to Net Zero. Nature-based Solutions (NbS) offer a promising way to address these issues, providing co-benefits for climate adaptation, food production, and ecosystem restoration. However, the implementation of NbS remains fragmented, unstrategic, and underfunded. The interdisciplinary Joined Up Landscapes (JUL) research project, funded by UKRI and Defra, aims to strengthen the contribution of NbS to climate adaptation in the context of UK food systems. This article presents an outline of the JUL project. JUL is structured around five interconnected work packages alongside three case studies demonstrating a range of agricultural NbS, including wetlands, floodplain mosaics, and catchment-scale habitat restoration. Preliminary findings highlight the importance of local context, stakeholder engagement, and flexible funding. JUL aims to inform policy, empower practitioners, and support a more climate-resilient UK food system.

items.title: Plastic pollution in Brazilian fish: distribution, risk factors, and implications across inland and coastal waters.
items.abstract: The contamination of aquatic environments by microplastics (MPs) represents a growing threat to biodiversity and ecosystem health. In Brazil, which hosts the world's richest freshwater fish fauna and high marine diversity, understanding MP contamination in fish is essential for ecological risk assessment and food security. This study presents a systematic review of MP contamination in Brazilian fish communities following PRISMA guidelines. From 26,878 records, 72 studies were selected, covering 15,809 individuals from 344 species, of which 5,182 (32.7%) contained MPs. Contamination occurred across all trophic guilds and water column strata. Studies were mainly concentrated in the Amazon and Paraná river basins and in the Northeast and Southeast marine regions. Fibres and fragments were the predominant particle types, mainly blue and black, composed primarily of polyethylene terephthalate (PET), polyamide (PA), and polyethylene (PE). Contamination levels were not significantly associated with trophic guild or water column position, but varied significantly by region, indicating that geographic factors play a greater role than trophic ecology in shaping MP patterns. Methodological heterogeneity across studies, including inconsistent digestion protocols and limited chemical confirmation, constrains comparability. Overall, MP contamination in Brazilian fish is widespread and geographically structured, highlighting the need for standardised monitoring protocols and broader geographic research to support effective environmental policies.

items.title: Genomic signatures of recent human adaptation to the foraging-to-farming transition.
items.abstract: Human populations across multiple regions transitioned from hunting and foraging to sedentary farming societies starting from ~10 thousand years ago (ka) to 12 ka, narrowing dietary diversity and transforming relationships with animals and pathogens. Here, to investigate how these ecological changes shaped human adaptations, we analysed high-coverage whole-genome sequence data from 1,092 individuals practising hunter-gatherer, agriculturalist and pastoralist lifestyles across 8 geographic regions spanning Africa, Asia and Oceania. Haplotype-based scans revealed pervasive recent positive selection on regulatory variation and genes associated with immune function across all subsistence modes, challenging the notion that agriculturalists alone experienced uniquely strong pathogenic pressures. By explicitly modelling correlations between allele frequencies and subsistence strategy, we uncovered convergent adaptations at a cross-continental scale in pathways beyond immunity, including metabolic, spermatogenesis and developmental pathways, supporting the life history hypothesis that energy allocation to growth, reproduction and maintenance shifted with the adoption of agriculture. Collectively, our findings illuminate the genetic legacy of ecological changes associated with the foraging-to-farming transition and highlight the central role of non-coding regulatory variation in human adaptation.

items.title: Closest relatives of poxviruses prevail in human and animal guts worldwide.
items.abstract: Large and giant double-stranded DNA viruses substantially affect eukaryotic ecology and evolution 1-4 . They prevail in the environment but are rarely found in the digestive system of animals 5,6 . Here we present the discovery of a diversified group of DNA viruses with large linear genomes, dubbed egoviruses, that comprise a putative viral order most closely related to animal-infecting poxviruses. Egoviruses are found worldwide, almost exclusively in the digestive system of humans, livestock and wild animals. The most prevalent human-specific egovirus is spread across continents, demonstrating a long-term association between egoviruses and the human gut microbiome. Eukaryotic homologues of egovirus core genes suggest that these viruses primarily infect Trichostomatia (ciliates), which assist ruminant digestive processes 7 , and Parabasalia (Metamonada), which influence animal immunity and gut microbiome ecology 8 . Egoviruses also contributed to the genetic makeup of polintons, endogenous viruses that proliferated in genomes of Trichomonas vaginalis 9 and its close Parabasalia relatives. Unlike poxviruses that form brick-shaped virions, egoviruses are predicted to form multilayered icosahedral capsids resembling those of asfuviruses and probably representing the ancestral virion structure. Egoviruses are the only known clade of double-stranded DNA viruses of eukaryotes prevailing in the animal digestive system. Phylogenomic analysis suggests an evolutionary scenario whereby egovirus-like ancestors of poxviruses infected anaerobic unicellular eukaryotes inside the gut of ancestral animals, before transitioning to animal cell infection, which was accompanied by the virion metamorphosis.

items.title: Injury-induced signalling coordinates immunity and cannibalism in locusts.
items.abstract: Cannibalism, the consumption of conspecifics, is widespread across the animal kingdom and can profoundly influence individual fitness and population dynamics 1,2 . Although the ecological and social conditions that favour cannibalism have been well documented 2 , the molecular signals that trigger cannibalistic attacks have remained poorly understood. Here we show that in Locusta migratoria, guaiacol, a volatile compound with augmented release after injury, attracts gregarious nymphs and induces cannibalistic behaviour. Guaiacol is detected by olfactory receptors LmOR36 and LmOR34, and disruption of either receptor abolishes attraction, thereby impairing induction of cannibalism. Guaiacol is synthesized by haemolymph symbiont Enterobacter hormaechei. Injury promotes bacterial congregation at the wound site, leading to elevated guaiacol production through a clustered set of vanillic acid decarboxylase genes; deletion of this gene cluster abolishes guaiacol production and its behavioural effects. Notably, guaiacol initially functions as a beneficial signal after injury. Guaiacol activates immune-related pathways in wounded locusts, enhancing pathogen resistance and increasing survival following minor injury. However, when guaiacol emission exceeds a threshold determined by injury severity, it functions as an external cue that attracts cannibals. Cannibalistic locusts exploit this immune-related odour to locate severely injured conspecifics, gaining both nutritional resources and immune system benefits. Together, our findings identify a microbial-chemical mechanism that links immune defence with cannibalistic behaviour and provide potential molecular targets for manipulation of cannibalism-dependent population dynamics.

items.title: Global patterns and drivers of bee richness and endemism on islands.
items.abstract: Islands account for a disproportionate share of global biodiversity 1 , yet insects, including invaluable pollinators such as bees 2 , remain underrepresented in island biogeography research 3 . Here we present a global checklist of island bees, recording 4,147 species across 305 islands. Although islands comprise only about 6% of the Earth's land area, they support around 20% of known global bee diversity, and 42% of insular species are endemic, making up around 8% of all known bee species. Island bee species richness peaks at mid-latitudes (at least in the Northern Hemisphere), mirroring continental trends 4 . Native richness increases with island area and declines with isolation, consistent with patterns in other taxa 5 . The strength of island species-area relationships varies among biomes and is steepest in Mediterranean-type systems, which also support disproportionately high bee richness relative to flowering plant diversity. The number of endemic species is highest on large tropical islands, reflecting extensive in situ diversification. Major centres of bee endemism include Madagascar, Malesia (the Greater Sundas and New Guinea) and the Hawaiian islands, where a single large radiation of Hylaeus (Nesoprosopis) dominates 6 . Among islands that are capable of supporting endemic species, endemism scales strongly with total richness. These findings highlight the need to integrate island bee diversity into global conservation planning and position bees as a model for understanding insect evolution and conservation on islands.

items.title: Tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity.
items.abstract: Tropical land-use intensification threatens global biodiversity, yet most assessments of tropical agricultural landscapes focus on local-scale biodiversity, overlooking how land use restructures biodiversity across space and multiple taxa. Here we provide an ecosystem-wide assessment of 24 taxonomic groups across all domains of life-encompassing 40,049 species-along a land-use intensification gradient from lowland forests to intensively managed smallholder cash-crop monocultures in Indonesian landscapes. Despite widespread losses of landscape and local multidiversity 1 in monocultures (approximately 78% and 50%, respectively), we found no evidence for consistent community homogenization with land-use intensification. Instead, monocultures exhibit a systematic shift from turnover to nestedness for aboveground taxa. Such patterns of differentiation may mask trajectories towards biotic homogenization via early stages of assemblage simplification. Biotic differentiation has the potential to partly mitigate biodiversity losses by positively affecting γ-diversity. This opens management options, including the conservation of existing remnants of traditional agriculture and the implementation of sustainable management practices 2-4 . Our results demonstrate that tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity not only through species loss, but also via a pervasive reorganization of community composition across trophic levels. Conserving tropical biodiversity, therefore, requires a multi-taxon, landscape-scale perspective that explicitly integrates agricultural land uses with the protection of natural and semi-natural habitats to reconcile agricultural production and conservation.

items.title: Widespread deciduousness reveals diverse Amazonian phenological strategies.
items.abstract: The Amazon rainforest is a cornerstone of regional and global carbon cycling 1 and is widely regarded and modelled as a perennially evergreen ecosystem 2,3 . This prevailing view, however, masks substantial fine-scale variation in leaf phenology, limiting our capacity to predict ecosystem responses to climate change. Here by combining 10-m Sentinel-2 observations with machine learning, we uncover pervasive, spatially structured seasonal deciduousness across the basin. In 70.0% of the Amazon, leaf shedding precedes leaf flushing by at least 3 months, creating pronounced asynchrony between deciduousness and greenness seasonality, whereas the remainder shows near-synchronous phenology. Hydroclimate emerges as the dominant factor associated with this asynchrony across 51.6% of the area, followed by soil properties (33.2%) and light availability (15.2%). Motivated by this widespread decoupling between deciduousness and canopy greenness, we incorporated deciduousness-constrained leaf turnover and the resulting leaf-age demography into ecophysiological models, yielding spatially widespread improvements in the seasonal agreement between simulated gross primary productivity and satellite-derived photosynthetic seasonality across 79.9% of the basin. These findings challenge the conventional view of Amazonian phenology, demonstrating that previously overlooked deciduousness influences Amazonian carbon dynamics. Incorporating these insights into process-based models is essential for refining projections of climate-forest feedbacks in the Amazon and for understanding its ecological functions under accelerating global change.

items.title: Experimental disturbance-induced functional shifts in protected soft-sediment benthic communities.
items.abstract: Benthic communities form the foundation of food webs in coastal and shelf seas worldwide. However, these communities face severe threats from anthropogenic bottom-disturbing activities. Marine protected areas (MPAs) effectively safeguard benthic communities against such disturbances. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of MPAs in recovering benthic communities in highly dynamic soft-bottom areas is widely debated, as these communities are thought to be adapted to natural dynamics and therefore resistant to human impacts. In this study, we examined whether MPAs in highly dynamic seas support sensitive communities that are affected by bottom-disturbing fishing gear. Utilizing a before-after, control-impact (BACI) experimental design, we investigated the effects of disturbance caused by shrimp trawl gear on macrozoobenthic communities within MPAs in a dynamic coastal soft-bottom sea over 2 years. We assessed changes in taxonomic and functional diversity and community composition across three levels of trawling intensity and frequency (low intensity and high frequency, high intensity and low frequency, and high intensity and high frequency) and compared the changes with those in undisturbed control areas. The study was carried out in the less dynamic areas of the study system, where we found that even lighter gear altered functional diversity and community composition, whereas taxonomic diversity was unaffected. Taxonomic and functional turnover increased most under frequent disturbance. Moreover, disturbance reduced the recovery of long-lived species, whereas scavengers and predators increased at the cost of suspension feeders. Our findings demonstrate that anthropogenic disturbance remains a relevant ecological pressure, even in areas that appear resilient through their dynamic nature, and thus, MPAs provide ecological benefits by protecting sensitive and functionally important species. As taxonomic metrics fail to detect these changes, impact assessments and MPA management should incorporate functional traits to better evaluate protection effectiveness and identify communities and ecological functions that require targeted conservation.

items.title: Growth-reproduction trade-offs in woody plants are common but changing: a meta-analysis.
items.abstract: Growth and reproduction draw on a common resource pool, yet empirical studies of woody plants report widely differing relationships between seed production and growth. We synthesized 685 estimates from 78 studies covering 79 woody species, with study locations concentrated at northern temperate latitudes, to test how growth-reproduction correlations vary across time, species, and environments. Growth and reproduction measured within the same year were negatively correlated, suggesting an immediate cost of reproduction. Given the limited and uneven taxonomic sampling, phylogenetic patterns in growth-reproduction correlations remain uncertain. The correlations were not systematically related to functional traits or climate. Trade-offs were strongest in species with high interannual variability in seed production and weakened markedly over recent decades in these species. Together, these results show that growth-reproduction trade-offs in woody plants are common but not fixed, and that shifts in reproductive variability under environmental change can alter how trees balance growth and reproduction, with consequences for long-term forest functioning.

items.title: Beyond B-DNA: the biology of Z-DNA and Z-RNA recognition.
items.abstract: Z-DNA and Z-RNA (Z-NAs) have long been regarded as rare alternative structures of uncertain in vivo relevance. However, accumulating evidence demonstrates their formation across diverse biological systems. Only a limited number of proteins have been validated as direct, conformation-selective Z-NA binders. Proteins may also stabilize Z-states or promote transitions into or out of them, respond to the surrounding topological conditions, or associate indirectly with Z-prone loci. In this article, we propose five potentially overlapping modes of engagement for Z-NA-associated proteins: conformation readers, stabilizers, conformational remodelers, topology-coupled factors, and context-dependent interactors. By linking canonical Zα readers with topoisomerases, chromatin factors, immune sensors, and viral antagonists, this framework provides a basis for mechanistic classification, experimental validation, and future discovery.

items.title: Lactiplantibacillus plantarum in vegetable food waste valorization: A Swiss army knife spanning plant polysaccharide transformation and comprehensive metabolic versatility.
items.abstract: Lactic acid bacteria (LAB), particularly Lactiplantibacillus plantarum (formerly Lactobacillus plantarum), are promising microbial platforms for the sustainable bioconversion and valorization of vegetable food wastes and agro-industrial residues. Their metabolic versatility and adaptability allow them to transform plant-derived biomass into diverse value-added bioproducts, supporting circular bioeconomy and biorefinery strategies. While previous studies have extensively addressed L. plantarum genetic diversity, health effects and role in food fermentation, increasing attention has turned on its application in biomass utilization and waste-to-value processes. This review critically examines current efforts to employ L. plantarum in plant waste valorization, identifying major technological and biological bottlenecks while highlighting opportunities for a more rational exploitation of this species in bioconversion processes. However, the limited integration of genomic and functional data remains a key obstacle to developing more efficient and predictable valorization strategies. To complement the literature analysis, a pan-genome exploration of 348 publicly available genomes was conducted, focusing on carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes) as an example of how genomic information may support strain selection and process design. This analysis revealed a conserved genetic core alongside a highly variable accessory genome, together with pronounced differences among strains in their CAZyme repertoires. This genomic diversity suggests substantial variation in carbohydrate-processing potential and may contribute to differences in fermentation performance across different matrices. While these observations require experimental validation and cannot directly predict performance in complex substrates, they illustrate how genome-informed approaches may help guide future screening strategies beyond the largely empirical methods currently reported.

items.title: Genetic diversity, selective constraint and phylogenetic signal of the melanocortin 1 receptor (MC1R) gene across Lagomorpha.
items.abstract: Coat color contributes to camouflage and fitness in mammals, yet the adaptative and evolutionary variation of the melanocortin-1 receptor (MC1R) gene, a key gene in pigmentation, remains incompletely characterized across Lagomorpha. We sequenced the complete 954-bp MC1R coding region in 19 species representing 14 Leporidae (Bunolagus monticularis, Lepus californicus, L. castroviejoi, L. capensis, L. europaeus, L. granatensis, L. saxatilis, L. timidus, L. townsendii, Oryctolagus cuniculus, Pentalagus furnessi, Romerolagus diazi, Sylvilagus floridanus, and S. nuttallii) and five Ochotonidae (Ochotona alpina, O. dauurica, O. hyperborea, O. macrotis, and O. pusilla) and compared the resulting alleles with public sequences. The diversity dataset comprised 21 haplotypes (Hd = 0.987), with 249 variable sites and marked sequence divergence between families (F ST = 0.667). Codon-based analyses showed significantly lower nonsynonymous than synonymous substitution rates in Leporidae, Ochotonidae and the complete dataset, indicating purifying selection and strong functional constraint. Phylogenetic analyses consistently separated Leporidae from Ochotonidae, although relationships among recently diverged Lepus species were weakly resolved. Most intraspecific polymorphisms were synonymous, whereas only a limited number of missense variants were detected. Unique amino acid substitutions in the dark-coated Pentalagus furnessi and Romerolagus diazi are of particular interest as candidate pigmentation variants, although their functional effects require experimental validation. Overall, MC1R combines substantial phylogenetic signal at deeper taxonomic levels with limited resolution of recent divergences, while its coding sequence remains strongly constrained. These data provide a comparative framework for future functional, population genetic and phylogenomic studies of pigmentation and evolution in lagomorphs.

items.title: Size-Divergent Contributors and Interactions to PM Oxidative Potential: EC-Organics Additivity and Ion-Metal Synergy.
items.abstract: Atmospheric particulate matter (PM), with complex physicochemical properties such as composition and size, poses serious health risks. Oxidative potential (OP) is considered a key factor in PM's health effects, but its relationship with PM properties and sources remains unclear. This study investigated approximately 100 PM components (environmental and bioaccessible concentrations) across nine size fractions using ion chromatography, carbon analysis, inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectrometer, and gas chromatograph-mass spectrometer. OP was detected by dithiothreitol (DTT) assay, and bioaccessibility was evaluated using simulated epithelial lung fluid (SELF). The dominant components and their interactions were found to be different across sizes. Fine PM OP is mainly driven by elemental carbon (EC), organic compounds (e.g., 9,10-phenanthrenequinone), and ions, while coarse PM OP is dominated by bioaccessible metals (e.g., Ni, Cu, As, Mn). Integrating ambient data and experimental validation, we find interactions among components: additive effects of EC and 9,10-phenanthrenequinone with high intrinsic OP dominate in fine particles, while in coarse fractions, ions drive OP enhancement by facilitating metal bioaccessibility. Furthermore, it's found that bioaccessibility greatly affects the contribution of metals to OP but has limited impact on organics. By integrating positive matrix factorization (PMF) and an extreme gradient boosting model combined with SHapley Additive exPlanations (XGBoost-SHAP), this study evaluates how PM sources influence OP. Key sources contributing to OP vary by size: traffic, secondary aerosols, and combustion show greater relative importance in predicting OP V in PM V in PM 2.1-3.3 ; traffic and dust are among the more influential sources in PM 3.3-10 . This study provides the first comprehensive evidence that the key components and their interactions associated with OP differ across sizes.

items.title: A Risk-Aware and Low-Cost Machine Learning Framework for Predicting Reaction Rate Constants of Organic Pollutants: A Case Study of the SO<sub>4</sub>•<sup>-</sup> System.
items.abstract: Machine learning shows promise for predicting the reaction rate constants of organic pollutants in advanced oxidation processes. However, existing studies face bottlenecks in handling heterogeneous kinetic data, the trade-off between feature cost and mechanistic insight, and prediction uncertainty. To address these challenges, we used the sulfate radical (SO 4 • - ) system as a representative case study and established a standardized curation workflow for heterogeneous literature data, developed an ensemble learning model using low-cost molecular descriptors, and integrated conformal prediction with applicability domain analysis to unify point predictions, uncertainty intervals, and applicability-domain boundaries. The model achieved R 2 = 0.9213, RMSE = 0.3414, and MAE = 0.1775 on the random test set, and retained predictive ability under a scaffold-based split (R 2 = 0.7098, RMSE = 0.6541, and MAE = 0.4995), although with substantially increased error relative to the random split. Meta-level cross-fitted adaptive conformal prediction achieved 93.3% empirical coverage under the random split but decreased to 91.3% under scaffold-based extrapolation, indicating that nominal intervals should be interpreted jointly with applicability-domain information for structurally novel compounds. SHAP analysis identified aromaticity, polarizability, and charge distribution as key drivers, while error attribution revealed three failure modes: data heterogeneity, low-similarity scaffold extrapolation, and chemistry/condition-sensitive systems. A visual online prediction platform was also developed. This risk-aware framework provides decision support for reactivity assessment of organic pollutants in advanced oxidation processes by combining generalizability, interpretability, and uncertainty quantification.

items.title: Survival and swim speed performance of Alewife, a small, laterally compressed prey fish, following acoustic transmitter implantation.
items.abstract: Alewife (Alosa pseudoharengus) is a small, pelagic fish that is an important prey source for piscivores in the Laurentian Great Lakes, yet its spatial ecology is poorly known, which limits the ability to monitor populations. Acoustic telemetry is a tool to understand spatial ecology; however, there may be tagging effects on a smaller body-sized population of Alewife where tag burden is higher than in larger-bodied marine populations. We assessed survival, swimming abilities and healing of Alewife from Lake Ontario after acoustic transmitter implantation. In a laboratory setting, tagged Alewife were compared across tag sizes (Innovasea models V6 and V7-4x), controls and shams (surgery conducted with no tag implantation) in fall 2024 (n = 76). Tagging survival was also assessed in spring 2025 (variety of V7 tags) when Alewife had developed gonads and across sex (n = 126). Capture, transport and laboratory introduction resulted in moderate mortality in fall 2024 (40%), which was reduced in spring 2025 (4%), an improvement we attribute to the refined protocols reported here. Post-treatment (transmitter, sham, control) survival was high (100% in fall; 91% in spring) with tag burdens from 2 to 8%. We attribute lower spring survival to gonad development, but it was also influenced significantly by a holding tank effect. Two weeks post-tagging, Alewife achieved critical swimming speeds of 37.9 ± 7.6 cm s -1 , with no significant differences among treatments. Incisions were all scored as moderately to highly healed 2 weeks post-surgery. Our findings establish the feasibility of tagging smaller, freshwater Alewife with acoustic tags, following best practices reported here, for telemetry applications in the Great Lakes to better understand the spatial ecology of this lower trophic species of major management and ecosystem importance.

items.title: Disentangling intrinsic and extrinsic drivers of gill ectoparasitism in an endemic North African leuciscid.
items.abstract: Seasonal variation in fish parasite burden reflects the interplay between parasite transmission, environmental conditions and host characteristics, yet the relative contributions of these factors remain incompletely understood in many wild freshwater fishes. We investigated gill ectoparasitism in the Maghrebian Bleak (Tropidophoxinellus callensis), a freshwater fish endemic to Algeria and Tunisia, examining variation in parasite burden in relation to season, host age, physiological condition and dietary breadth. Three ectoparasite taxa were identified, Gyrodactylus barbi, Trichodina sp. and Dactylogyrus fraternus, providing the first characterisation of the gill ectoparasite assemblage of this species. Parasite burden peaked in summer, and season remained significantly associated with ectoparasitism after accounting for host characteristics, although much of the explained variation was shared among predictors. Parasite abundance increased with host age in unadjusted analyses, but the relationship reversed after accounting for hepatic condition and other predictors. Furthermore, parasite burden exhibited a nonlinear relationship with hepatic condition, reaching its highest values at intermediate hepatosomatic indices. These findings demonstrate that seasonal variation in ectoparasitism is closely intertwined with host ontogeny and physiological condition, highlighting the importance of considering intrinsic and extrinsic factors jointly when investigating host-parasite relationships.

items.title: Quantifying time-dependent meteorological controls on lake eutrophication through cumulative-hysteresis response mapping: Evidence from Erhai Lake.
items.abstract: Lake eutrophication can respond to meteorological drivers through both cumulative and hysteresis (C&H) effects, but these time-dependent effects are difficult to identify with conventional correlations or fixed-lag analyses. This study proposed a cumulative-hysteresis response mapping to identify the sensitive climate factors and determine the influencing time window on lake eutrophication. Specifically, a C&H matrix of a meteorological indicator and its C&H effect matrix was constructed. The C&H effect matrix, a three-dimensional dataset comprising cumulative days, hysteresis days, and correlation parameters, was used to screen meteorological indicators (SMIs). Regression models incorporating SMIs and the trophic level index (TLI) were further developed to evaluate predictive performance. The proposed approach was applied to Erhai Lake in the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau. Seven categories of SMIs were identified: radiation, precipitation, evaporation, wind field, temperature, humidity, and air pressure. Their cumulative effect windows ranged from 71.25 to 149 days, while hysteresis windows ranged from 29.25 to 194.08 days. Temperature, air pressure, humidity, and evaporation had a positive effect on TLI. In contrast, radiation, precipitation, and the wind-field variables showed negative effects. Regression models based on the 7 SMIs were developed to simulate variations in TLI. The model achieves satisfactory performance in reproducing whole-lake TLI and adequately captures the temporal trends of TLI across the 11 investigated sites. These results demonstrate that the cumulative-hysteresis response mapping can effectively identify key meteorological drivers and their response windows.The identified sensitive meteorological indicators further facilitate meteorology-informed evaluation of lake eutrophication risk.

items.title: Which Fruit Traits Correlate Reliably With Sugar Content, and Does This Vary With Dispersal Syndrome?
items.abstract: Deciding which fruits to eat, and when, is a key decisions made by frugivores, with implications for animal nutrition, seed dispersal, and other ecosystem interactions. It has long been hypothesized that fruit traits, including color, odor, and hardness, are adapted to attract different guilds of frugivores (e.g., birds versus mammals) and facilitate fruit foraging through signaling of ripeness and nutritional reward via different sensory modalities. Yet how various traits change during ripening in fruits with different putative dispersal syndromes is poorly understood. We predicted visual traits to be more correlated with changes in sugar content during ripening in a bird-consumed fruit and odor and hardness traits to be correlated with sugar content in mammal-consumed fruits. We measured color via image analysis, odor via solid-phase microextraction GC-MS, hardness via a portable mechanical tester, and sugar content using a digital refractometer in n = 100 bananas ( Musa acuminata ) and n = 160 mangoes ( Mangifera indica ), two large, climacteric fruits as models of mammal-dispersed fruits, and in n = 80 black currants ( Ribes nigrum ), a small, non-climacteric berry as a model for bird-dispersed fruit. Bananas, and to a lesser extent mangoes, tend to get softer, have higher red-green and lower blue-yellow chromaticity values, and become more odorous as they get sweeter. Currants get softer, darker, have lower red-green and higher blue-yellow chromaticity values, and become less odorous as they become sweeter. Our results suggest that some traits, such as color and odor, may vary among plant taxa with different dispersal syndromes, while other traits, such as fruit softening, may be more consistently associated with fruit ripening when they occur. We have developed a tractable framework for assessing multimodal plant cues and signals and hope this research inspires future studies of greater taxonomic diversity.

items.title: Unsupervised Selective Labeling for Semi-Supervised Aerial Imagery Recognition.
items.abstract: Traditional aerial wildlife monitoring surveys rely on rapid visual identification and counting by expert biologists from moving aircraft. Modern camera systems mounted on survey aircraft are now being deployed to collect large datasets of imagery that provide a persistent, reusable snapshot of wildlife populations. Manual analysis of these extensive datasets can overwhelm the staffing of natural resource agencies, especially for large-scale surveys. Deep learning systems are being investigated as a potential solution to automate analysis, but significant human effort is still required to curate a labeled dataset for model training. To address this challenge, we propose Semi-Supervised Aerial Imagery Recognition (referred to as SSAR), a framework that minimizes annotation effort while maintaining classification performance. The key of SSAR is to select the best subset of images for annotation while leveraging the hidden information from the remaining unlabeled data. Concretely, SSAR integrates three components: (1) unsupervised feature learning tailored to aerial imagery to capture ecologically meaningful visual patterns, (2) unsupervised selective labeling that prioritizes representative and diverse images for annotation, and (3) semi-supervised classification that incorporates the remaining unlabeled images during training. We evaluate SSAR on wildlife recognition case studies using object-centric image crops from high-resolution aerial imagery collected over the United States Atlantic Outer Continental Shelf (OCS) and the Great Lakes region, comprising 57,265 images across 11 coarse categories. Using only 6.4% labeled data, SSAR matches the fully supervised macro accuracy of 85.0% achieved with 100% labeled data and further surpasses it by reaching 86.8% with 12.8% labeled data. These results demonstrate that SSAR enables accurate and scalable aerial wildlife recognition with an order-of-magnitude reduction in manual annotation.

items.title: Foraging Habits and Habitats of the Indian Swiftlet (Aerodramus unicolor), in Maharashtra, India.
items.abstract: Specialized aerial insectivores, such as swifts and swiftlets, are essential for sustaining ecosystem equilibrium by regulating insect populations. Despite their ecological significance, the foraging ecology of many swiftlets remains understudied. Therefore, we aimed to understand the foraging extent, habits, and habitat of the Indian Swiftlet. We conducted this study between January and December 2022 across seven representative habitats in Sindhudurg, Maharashtra. We collected the primary data through a presence survey, while the secondary data were sourced from GBIF.org. Distance matrix analysis was used to estimate the foraging extent at the regional and global levels. We used a scan sampling method to document foraging habits and a handheld environmental meter to record microclimatic variables. We documented the tree composition at every foraging site using quadrat sampling. The proximity of their breeding colonies primarily influences the Indian Swiftlet's foraging range, extending up to 20 km in Sindhudurg and over 80 km from the known breeding sites in India and Sri Lanka. Over 715 h of observations (2860 sets each of 10 min) revealed 15 different foraging habits of the Indian Swiftlet. The species prominently uses wetlands surrounded by agricultural lands and plantation areas as primary habitats, whereas the rocky shores and lateritic plateaus were avoided. Out of all the microclimatic drivers, relative humidity influences flutter activity in the swiftlets, which corresponds to the feeding maneuver. This study contributed to understanding the foraging dynamics of the Indian Swiftlet in Sindhudurg. It also highlighted the importance of wetlands in sustaining swiftlet populations and the need to prioritize habitats for conservation in the face of habitat degradation and a changing climate.

items.title: Toward standard testing methods in biophotovoltaics based on cyanobacteria.
items.abstract: Microbial biophotovoltaics (BPVs) are an emerging renewable energy technology that harnesses photosynthetic microorganisms to generate electric current. Despite the rapid growth of the field, the lack of standardized testing and reporting methods currently prevents the benchmarking of devices, slowing technological progress. This article provides a critical analysis of the experimental practices used in BPV research, highlighting the significant variability in device configurations, light sources, electrode materials, biomass quantification methods, and electrochemical measurement protocols reported in the literature. It further considers the historical standardization of protocols for conventional photovoltaics (PVs) and the resulting acceleration of the maturation and market adoption of PV technologies. Drawing inspiration from conventional PVs, the article outlines key steps toward BPV standardization, including defining common testing conditions, methods for data normalization, shared reference systems, and round-robin testing protocols. Establishing consensus in the testing protocols would significantly improve reproducibility and enable meaningful comparisons across laboratories, accelerating the development and deployment of BPVs.

items.title: Collective Movement in the Wintering Oriental Storks (Ciconia boyciana): Longer Food Handling Time Is Associated With Successful Initiation.
items.abstract: Collective movement is a widespread phenomenon among social animals and plays a key role in shaping both individual fitness and population dynamics. By enabling individuals to exploit social information from conspecifics, collective movement can improve foraging efficiency, reduce predation risk, and facilitate coordinated decision-making. Despite growing interest in collective movements, studies on waterbirds remain limited, largely because tracking individual level traits and social relationships in large, mobile populations is difficult. In this study, we examined the effects of individual behavioral characteristics, flock characteristics, and position within a flock on the collective movement of Oriental Storks ( Ciconia boyciana ) in winter from 2024 to 2025, controlling for the effects of other variables (winter period and habitat type). Our results show that individuals who spent more time tracking and handling food resources were more likely to become leaders during collective movements. We found that initiation success was positively associated with the initiator's food handling time and flock size, whereas successful foraging rate, failed foraging rate, locomotion rate, and flock position were not independently associated with initiation success after adjustment for the flock-level, temporal, and habitat variables. Among successful initiation events, movement duration increased with food handling time but decreased with flock size. Successful foraging rate, failed foraging rate, locomotion rate, and flock position were not independently associated with movement duration. Therefore, our study demonstrates that storks exhibiting these foraging patterns were more likely to act as unintentional leaders when initiating collective movement, and these individuals typically exhibited longer food handling times. Further studies using marking and GPS tracking are needed to identify which individual traits most strongly influence follower responses and to clarify how social interactions shape decision-making and the maintenance of collective movements.

items.title: By Land or By Sea: Ecology in a Foreign (Scot)Land
items.abstract: Biology has taken me from studying coastal mangrove ecosystems in South Florida to surveying ancient temperate rainforests in the Scottish Highlands. In this talk, I'll share the windy path that connected those two very different worlds and the unconventional experiences that shaped my path toward a career in ecology. I'll discuss how undergraduate research opened the door to scientific discovery, why I chose to spend two years traveling across the United States after graduation before pursuing graduate school, and what ultimately led me across the Atlantic to the University of Edinburgh. Along the way, I'll introduce my current dissertation research on Scotland's Atlantic temperate rainforests, where I study how herbivore impacts influence communities of rare rainforest lichens, remarkable organisms that serve as important indicators of forest health. This presentation will focus on the many paths a career in biology can take. I'll share what it's like to conduct ecological fieldwork in Scotland, the realities of graduate school abroad, and the lessons I've learned about embracing uncertainty, seeking opportunities, and following your curiosity. Whether your interests lie on land, beneath the sea, or somewhere above or in between, I hope this talk demonstrates that the path to your goals doesn't have to be a straight line. About the presenter Joe Dubner is an MSc student in Ecology, Evolution and Biodiversity at the University of Edinburgh and an aquarist at Scotland's National Aquarium. He earned dual Bachelor of Science degrees in Biology and Marine Biology from Nova Southeastern University in 2023, where he was also a Razor's Edge Research Scholar. Through RER, he conducted undergraduate research in marine biogeochemistry under Dr. Tyler Cyronak. During his undergraduate studies, Joe served as President of the Nature Club, chaired the Sustainability Club's Climate Change Committee, and was actively involved in science outreach and environmental initiatives. After graduating, Joe spent two years traveling throughout the United States as a professional petsitter and tutor, an unconventional experience that reinforced his passion for wildlife, conservation, and exploring new environments. In 2025, he moved to Scotland to continue his education at the University of Edinburgh. His current research focuses on Atlantic temperate rainforests, investigating how herbivore impacts influence epiphytic lichen communities in Scotland's internationally important rainforest ecosystems. Joe hopes to continue to ultimately build a career as a university professor, combining ecological research, teaching, and mentorship. The path there is not a straight line, and it doesn't have to be.

items.title: Compassionate technology in teacher education: Advancing connection, care, and digital wellbeing in a digital society
items.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies into teacher education has transformed teaching, learning, and professional preparation worldwide. While these innovations have enhanced accessibility, personalisation, collaboration, and instructional efficiency, they have also intensified concerns regarding techno-stress, digital fatigue, emotional disengagement, ethical dilemmas, and diminished human connection. These challenges highlight the need for educational approaches that balance technological advancement with compassion, inclusion, and digital wellbeing. This conceptual paper proposes a Human-Centred Framework for Digital Wellbeing in Teacher Education, developed through a critical synthesis of contemporary literature on compassionate pedagogy, ethical AI, digital wellbeing, inclusive education, and human-centred learning. The framework comprises five interconnected dimensions: Human-Centred AI Integration, Emotional and Psychological Wellbeing, Compassionate Pedagogical Practices, Inclusive and Equitable Digital Learning, and Ethical and Mindful Technology Engagement. Collectively, these dimensions position technology as a means of strengthening empathy, meaningful relationships, equity, and sustainable learning rather than merely improving efficiency. The paper discusses implications for teacher education curricula, digital pedagogy, institutional policy, and professional learning. It argues that preparing future teachers for AI-enabled classrooms requires not only digital competence but also the capacity to create ethical, inclusive, and compassionate learning environments that promote human flourishing in an increasingly digital society.

items.title: A Latent Variable Perspective on EEG Measures of Attentional Control
items.abstract: Attentional control is a core cognitive function, yet there is still a significant debate revolving around its definition, factorial structure and underlying neural mechanisms. Research in this domain has largely developed along two largely disconnected traditions. Psychometric approaches assess individual differences using latent-variable models (e.g., structural equation modeling, confirmatory factor analysis), while cognitive neuroscience focuses on group-level behavioral and neural effects. This raises a critical question: can neural measures robust at the group level validly capture stable individual differences? Or more specifically, can some of the principles and analytical methods adopted in individual-differences research be directly applied to neural correlates of attentional control? The current study aims to address this question. Electroencephalogram data were recorded from participants as they completed four attentional control paradigms: a change detection task, the go/no-go task, the Simon task, and the Stroop task. From each task, we extracted the P3 component and a data-driven decoding accuracy measure as indices of conflict processing and tested whether these neural measures load onto a common latent factor of attentional control. Results revealed weak and largely non-significant correlations. Structural-equation modeling provided no evidence for a common latent factor, despite robust within-task effects at the group level reflected both in the behavioral and the EEG parameters. These findings suggest that EEG components may lack the construct validity needed to reliably capture individual differences in attentional control.

items.title: Subtractive and Divisive Methods for Isolating Neural Oscillations From Broadband Activity Yield Different, Even Conflicting, Power Estimates
items.abstract: Understanding the role of oscillatory brain activity in cognition is a key objective in cognitive neuroscience. However, quantifying the power of narrowband neural oscillations is made challenging by the presence of non-oscillatory broadband activity in the signal. Recently, there has been a proliferation of methods designed to separate oscillatory from non-oscillatory (aperiodic) signals. To perform this separation, these methods must model the relationship between oscillatory and aperiodic components. Crucially, however, such methods rarely explicitly clarify whether they assume that this relationship is additive or multiplicative, an issue compounded by the common use of log-transformed data (i.e., subtraction in log space is equivalent to division in linear space). Here, we show the importance of justifying which assumption about component relations is applied. Using simulated power spectra with additive oscillatory and aperiodic components, we illustrate that methods that assume a multiplicative model, such as the popular specparam (formerly fooof) toolbox, systematically mis-estimate oscillatory activity in ways that can obscure real oscillatory differences between conditions, or even reverse their sign, creating an illusory effect. We then demonstrate these effects in two complementary empirical datasets: (a) a cross-sectional, between-subjects analysis of age-related differences in alpha power, showing how separation approaches impact effect size and detectability; and (b) a within-subjects analysis of pre-stimulus changes in alpha power in a detection task, showing how switching between approaches can greatly reduce the evidence for an effect, leading to different conclusions. These results highlight that researchers must explicitly report and justify assumptions about aperiodic and oscillatory signal combination, as these assumptions have implications not only for analyses of oscillatory activity and resultant conclusions, but also for integration of results across reports (which may implicitly employ different assumptions), and ultimately for the development of theories regarding electrophysiological features and their putative relations to cognition.

items.title: From Pipeline Automation to Scientific Discovery: A Multi-Layer Agent-Driven Bioinformatics Framework
items.abstract: Abstract AI-driven bioinformatics is undergoing a multi-layer evolution from script automation to autonomous scientific discovery. We present a three-layer agent-driven framework spanning this complete spectrum. Layer 1 (Foundation Validation) benchmarks three OpenClaw agents—DESeq2 differential expression, GO/KEGG enrichment, and variant calling—against standard pipelines on TCGA liver cancer and E. coli genomic data, achieving near-perfect padj correlation (r ~ 1.0), >90% pathway overlap, and 95.8% variant concordance. Layer 2 (Domain Tool) presents CRISPR Agent, a multi-layer pipeline integrating Cas-OFFinder candidate discovery, multi-backend off-target scoring (mm_only/CFD/MIT), genomic context annotation, and end-to-end report synthesis, validated on GUIDE-seq/CIRCLE-seq/CHANGE-seq benchmarks. Layer 3 (Scientific Discovery) introduces SciOS, a ten-agent autonomous discovery system governed by a five-gate FORUM review chain (Plan-Execute-Audit-Synthesize-Ratify). Deployed across three single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets (457,000 cells, 154,000 spatial spots), SciOS produced three findings: (i) effector genes encoding ion channels, synaptic adhesion, and axon guidance proteins are significantly more conserved across cortical regions than transcription factor identity genes (P = 1.2 x 10^-16, d = 1.27)—a genuinely novel discovery inverting the standard neuroscience hierarchy; (ii) APOE expression is spatially coupled to oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (r = 0.673) but not mature oligodendrocytes (r = 0.136) in the human entorhinal cortex; and (iii) independent pseudobulk validation of CALB1/SOX6 dopamine neuron depletion in Parkinson's disease. The framework's Critic agent mandated average confidence reductions of -0.06 across all claims, while a Literature agent corrected a directional error introduced by autonomous analysis without domain context. These three layers collectively define an evolution from "doing" to "designing" to "discovering," establishing a methodological foundation for fully autonomous scientific discovery systems.

items.title: Adolescent social isolation and re-socialization increases alcohol intake and aversion-resistant drinking in male and female rats.
items.abstract: Rationale Adverse experiences during adolescence, especially social isolation, increases risk for alcohol use disorders (AUDs). Previous rodent studies of adolescent social isolation (ASI) encompassed all stages of adolescence and/or maintained isolation into adulthood, limiting identification of vulnerable stages of adolescence. Utilizing males only, or combining the sexes, also may have contributed to contradictory findings. Objectives Investigate social isolation restricted to discrete adolescent stages in combination with re-socialization and then persistent alcohol drinking. Determine whether adolescent isolation during specific developmental time periods, with or without subsequent re-socialization, leads to increased alcohol drinking in males or females. Methods Male and female Wistar rats underwent one of six housing conditions: (1) isolation from postnatal day (P)21-42 followed by re-socialization (ASIR-Early), (2) isolation from P42-63 followed by re-socialization (ASIR-Late), or (3) continuous isolation from P21 onward (ASI), or (4​-6) one of three appropriate control treatments. Alcohol-related behaviors were assessed in adulthood using intermittent-access two-bottle choice drinking (IAP), limited daily access (LDA-20) procedures, quinine-adulterated aversion-resistant drinking (ARD), and alcohol re-exposure following prolonged abstinence. Results In general, ASIR-Early and ASI elevated alcohol drinking in males and females, when compared to contemporary controls, during IAP, LDA-20, ARD, and after prolonged withdrawal, while ASIR-Late had largely similar effects as control conditions. However, for females, only ASI led to greater ARD at the highest quinine dose and also increased alcohol drinking after prolonged withdrawal. In contrast, for males, ASIR-Early and ASI had largely similar enhancement of alcohol drinking. Conclusions Under these conditions, isolation housing that encompassed the early adolescent period produced enduring increases in alcohol-related behaviors, with re-socialization perhaps more protective in females against ARD and elevated intake after abstinence. These results inform future studies that will investigate neural mechanisms underlying ASI-induced enhancement of alcohol drinking.

items.title: Enhanced Groundwater Storage Drives Ecological Recovery in the Qaidam Basin Under Climate Change
items.abstract: Abstract Understanding climate-hydrology-ecology interactions in arid environments is critical for management of scarce water resources, yet the mechanisms through which climate change impacts groundwater storage and subsequently regulates ecosystem dynamics remain poorly quantified.
