items.title: Novel Insights Into the Life History, Taxonomy, Host Use, and Biogeography of the Rare Ant Social Parasite Acromyrmex argentinus (Gallardo) comb. nov.
items.abstract: Ant inquiline social parasites are brood parasites of free-living ant species that exploit the social colony services of their hosts for survival and reproduction. To trace the convergent evolutionary origins of inquiline social parasitism in ants, it is important to decipher the parasites' life histories. Here, we report novel observations on the rare inquiline social parasite Pseudoatta argentina Gallardo. In addition, we inferred a mitochondrial phylogeny for 15 leaf-cutting ant species. The phylogeny demonstrates that P. argentina is deeply nested inside the genus Acromyrmex rendering the genus Acromyrmex paraphyletic. On the basis of morphological and phylogenetic evidence, we synonymize the genus Pseudoatta under the name Acromyrmex . Our field study confirms that Acromyrmex argentinus (Gallardo) comb. nov . is an obligate, workerless inquiline social parasite of Acromyrmex leaf-cutting ants. We show that A. argentinus is likely monogynous, host-queen-intolerant, and reproduces semelparously. Winged males of A. argentinus are gynaecomorphic, that is, queen-like, and male and female offspring mate with their siblings. Mitochondrial DNA barcodes reveal that A. argentinus is highly inbred across its distribution, which was either caused by a genetic bottleneck during speciation or resulted from sib-mating. Acromyrmex argentinus is a generalist parasite exploiting at least four free-living Acromyrmex species including A. ambiguus , A. crassispinus , A. heyeri , and A. lundii . Furthermore, A. argentinus is distributed throughout northern-central Argentina, southern Brazil, and Uruguay, which constitutes the largest known geographic distribution range of any inquiline social parasite in the southern hemisphere. We suggest that repeated host shifts may have facilitated the geographic range expansion of the social parasite. Although widely distributed, A. argentinus is locally rare infecting ~1% of the colonies in a host population. In summary, our study suggests that the morphological, behavioral, and life history characters associated with the inquiline syndrome evolved convergently in a mosaic fashion across the fungus-growing ants.

items.title: Shifts in Biomass Allocation and Trait Correlations Under the Combined Effects of Drought and Shade.
items.abstract: Biomass allocation in plants is mainly interpreted through two major theories: Allometric Partitioning Theory (APT) and Optimal Partitioning Theory (OPT). Under a specific environmental condition where drought and shade co-occur, biomass allocation can also be explained by trade-off, facilitation, and uncoupled hypotheses. These theories and hypotheses make contradictory predictions regarding the direction of biomass allocation to above- versus belowground organs. Because empirical support can be found for each of them, it remains unresolved which framework better explains biomass allocation strategies under combined effects of drought and shade. Moreover, we lack a unified understanding of how these frameworks may integrate. To test these five frameworks, we examined three Fagaceae species with contrasting tolerances: drought-tolerant Quercus pubescens , shade-tolerant Fagus sylvatica , and Castanea sativa with moderate shade and drought tolerance. We conducted a greenhouse experiment to detect seedling responses to simulated drought and shade using an experimental design controlling water-table gradients, light quality and quantity. We analyzed aboveground growth via LiDAR, aboveground/belowground biomass allocations, and resource acquisition strategies of these three species. We found that individual seedling responses were highly nuanced along continuous gradients, and no single theory and hypothesis adequately explained the observed biomass allocation. Moreover, we developed a novel decision chart that systematically links these disparate theories and hypotheses, rather than treating them as mutually exclusive frameworks.

items.title: Comparisons of Food Intake Rate Between Wild and Game-Farm Mallards From North America.
items.abstract: Domesticated in Europe, the game-farm mallard has been released throughout North America over the last century to supplement wild mallard populations and to increase harvest opportunities. Recent landscape genomic studies have revealed that releases have resulted in geographically widespread introgressive hybridization between game-farm and wild mallards. As a result, there is increasing concern about possible negative effects of artificially selected game-farm genes moving into wild mallard populations in North America. Given the known differences in bill morphology between game-farm and wild mallards, we hypothesized that the food intake rate would differ between game-farm and wild mallards. We studied food intake rates of wild-caught and game-farm mallards in captivity by providing these birds a representative range of food sizes that wild mallards would normally consume. We detected that game-farm mallards ingested food at about half the rate of wild mallards. Our results suggest that game-farm introgression could lead to maladaptive traits in wild mallards, but an understanding of how game-farm traits may influence the survival and reproduction of wild × game-farm mallard hybrids is needed.

items.title: Dietary Composition Is Associated with Tissue Metal Concentrations in Two Sympatric Bats.
items.abstract: Most bats are insectivorous predators, serving as sensitive bioindicators for monitoring environmental heavy metal pollution. However, the link between trophic niche characteristics and heavy metal contaminant accumulation in wildlife remains poorly quantified. Here, we combined DNA metabarcoding of the cytochrome c oxidase subunit I ( COI ) gene with tissue-based heavy metal analyses to investigate dietary composition and its relationship with tissue metal concentrations in 2 coexisting bat populations, Myotis chinensis (Chiroptera: Vespertilionidae; n = 4) and Rhinolophus sinicus (Chiroptera: Rhinolophidae; n = 5). The results revealed significant dietary differentiation between the 2 bat populations. R. sinicus exhibited a highly concentrated dietary composition, with Endoclita davidi (Lepidoptera: Hepialidae) accounting for more than 99% of the prey-assigned sequencing reads. In contrast, M. chinensis showed a more diverse prey taxonomic composition, with sequencing reads primarily assigned to dipteran insects (Muscidae and Chironomidae), along with some lepidopterans. Multivariate ordination analyses further supported clear dietary differentiation at both the prey genus and species levels between the 2 bat populations. Significant differences in heavy metal concentrations were also observed between the 2 sampled populations. Dietary composition was associated with individual-level mean Cu concentrations, while tissue-specific associations varied among organs. Our findings suggest associations between dietary composition and tissue metal concentrations in the 2 sampled bat populations.

items.title: Psychometric Validation of the German International Depression Questionnaire and the International Anxiety Questionnaire.
items.abstract: Background The International Depression Questionnaire (IDQ) and the International Anxiety Questionnaire (IAQ) are brief, ICD-11-aligned self-report instruments designed to assess depressive episodes and generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). While the initial validation study of the original English versions supported unidimensional structures, further cross-cultural validation is warranted. This study examined the psychometric properties of the German versions of the IDQ and IAQ among German-speaking adults. Methods A total of 710 participants completed an online survey including the IDQ, IAQ, and additional measures assessing depressive symptoms, anxiety, posttraumatic stress, and adjustment difficulties. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses assessed factorial validity. Internal consistency was evaluated using Cronbach's alpha. Convergent and discriminant validity were examined via partial correlations controlling for age and gender. Results Analyses supported a three-factor structure for the IDQ (essential, cognitive-affective, and vegetative symptoms) and a unidimensional structure for the IAQ, as two-factor solutions yielded very highly correlated factors. Both scales demonstrated good model fit and excellent internal consistency ( α = 0.90 for each scale). The IDQ showed the strongest correlations with depressive symptoms and negative automatic thoughts, while the IAQ correlated most strongly with measures of generalized anxiety. Lower correlations with posttraumatic stress and adjustment problems supported discriminant validity. Conclusions The results provide initial evidence that the German versions of the IDQ and IAQ are reliable and valid tools for assessing ICD-11 depression and generalized anxiety. The multidimensional structure of the IDQ supports theoretical distinctions between depressive symptom domains, whereas the IAQ appears best represented by a single generalized anxiety factor. Further replication and validation against external clinical criteria are needed to establish the clinical relevance of these factor structures.

items.title: Hierarchical Control of Antiphase Synchronization in Biomorphic Spiking Neural Architectures for Locomotor Control
items.abstract: Central pattern generators (CPGs) provide a biologically inspired foundation for adaptive locomotor control, yet systematically characterizing their dynamic regimes in spiking neural networks remains challenging. This study introduces a framework for identifying and stabilizing antiphase synchronization in a biomorphic spiking CPG model embedded in a closed neuromuscular loop. A composite synchronization metric is developed, integrating phase coherence, amplitude balance, and temporal stability. Its performance is evaluated across systematically varied stimulation waveforms and synaptic configurations. Statistical analysis reveals that stimulation type dominates regime determination, with tonic drive yielding the most robust antiphase synchronization. Periodic inputs induce nonlinear saturation and context-dependent network routing. Although synaptic weights alone show limited discriminative power, they significantly modulate robustness within a given stimulation context, with reciprocal Ia interneuron connections emerging as key stabilizers. The proposed composite metric achieves robust antiphase detection, outperforming traditional phase-only measures while preserving biophysical interpretability. These findings establish a statistically validated, hierarchical modeling approach in which external drive defines the operating regime and targeted synaptic configurations fine-tune dynamic stability, providing actionable guidelines for closed-loop neuromechanical controllers and adaptive neuroprosthetic interfaces.

items.title: Birth position and tissue context influence Bipolar Cell translocation mode in the developing retina.
items.abstract: Neuronal translocation is essential for establishing functional tissue architecture in the developing central nervous system. While many of the cell-intrinsic mechanisms driving translocation have been identified, how these strategies adapt to dynamic developmental tissue changes remains less understood. Here, we address this question using retinal Bipolar Cells as a model as they are generated across unlaminated and laminated stages. This enables direct comparison of neuronal translocation modes and dynamics across development. We show that the mode of movement of Bipolar Cells changes depending on tissue lamination state. Bipolar Cells born before photoreceptor layer formation undergo directed, microtubule-dependent somal translocation as seen for other early born neurons. In contrast, later-born Bipolar Cells exhibit more passive and less directed displacement that seems to be mostly driven by collective tissue movements. Interference with tissue-wide movements reduces this displacement, while disrupting photoreceptor layer formation leads to directed translocation also at later developmental stages. Independent of strategy, cells achieve accurate laminar positioning. Together, this shows that tissue context can influence cell movement modes, a principle likely relevant across developing neural and other tissues.

items.title: GLP-1(9-37) Improves Left Ventricular Function in a Murine Model of Cardiac Pressure Overload by Promoting Mitochondrial Biogenesis.
items.abstract: Aim Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) is an incretin hormone that is released in response to nutrient intake and inflammation. Its active form, GLP-1(7-37), binds to the GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R), but GLP-1 is rapidly degraded by dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) into GLP-1(9-37), which does not bind to the classical GLP-1R. Both peptides exhibit cardioprotective effects, although the underlying mechanisms are unclear and the role of GLP-1(9-37) remains poorly understood. Methods and results In this study, we investigated cardiac and metabolic effects of GLP-1(9-37) in a mouse model of cardiac pressure overload. LacZ and GLP-1(9-37) were overexpressed using an AAV vector system. While GLP-1(9-37) does not affect glucose metabolism, it mechanistically activates key metabolic regulators, as evidenced by increased AMPK and PGC1α signalling. This shift suggests an improvement in cellular energy balance and mitochondrial function under hypertrophic stress conditions. GLP-1(9-37) was also found to mitigate adverse cardiac remodelling. Treatment is associated with reduced septal thickness and decreased cardiac fibrosis, indicating attenuation of structural hypertrophy. Conclusions In summary, our data suggest a protective role of GLP-1(9-37) in pressure-overload-induced cardiac remodelling, which is associated with AMPK/PGC1α-signalling.

items.title: Interpretation of non-statistically significant results in randomised controlled clinical trials in rehabilitation: a cross sectional analysis.
items.abstract: Objectives To assess the prevalence of misinterpretation of non-statistically significant results, both in the abstract and in the article conclusions, in a sample of randomized controlled trials with non-statistically significant primary outcomes published in rehabilitation journals, and the reporting of the primary outcomes in accordance with the CONSORT Guidelines. Methods A cross-sectional analysis was conducted of all RCTs with non-statistically significant primary outcomes in five general rehabilitation journals with the highest Impact Factor, published between 2019 and 2023. The objective of this analysis was to assess the prevalence of misinterpretation of non-statistically significant results, both in the abstract and in the article conclusions, in a sample of RCTs with non-statistically significant results and reporting of primary outcomes according to CONSORT guidelines. Results The analysis included 31 trials. The most common interpretation of non-statistically significant results was the evidence of absence, both in the abstract (74.2%) and the article (58.1%). Only four (12.9%) studies in the abstract and five (16.1%) conclusions in the article suggested the correct interpretation as the absence of evidence. Adherence to CONSORT guidelines was moderate, with only 61.3% of trials reporting results summaries for each arm, effect size, and confidence interval. Discussions/conclusions There is a need for increased rigor in reporting and interpreting non-statistically significant results in rehabilitation trials. Evidence misinterpretations can adversely impact clinical decision-making and future research directions. Efforts should be made to promote accurate interpretation of statistical results, emphasize the importance of analyzing confidence intervals, and develop educational interventions to improve statistical literacy.

items.title: Rapid turnover of corticosterone in humans.
items.abstract: Objective Adrenal insufficiency is primarily treated with replacement of cortisol, which is the predominant circulating glucocorticoid. Human adrenals also secrete corticosterone and emerging evidence suggests this may be a safer glucocorticoid replacement therapy. However, there is scant literature describing corticosterone physiology or potential pharmacokinetics in humans. Methods To investigate the secretion and metabolism of corticosterone in comparison with cortisol, we: 1) investigated daytime profiles of circulating cortisol/corticosterone in 7 healthy volunteers; 2) quantified metabolism of both hormones in vitro; 3) measured 24-hour urinary glucocorticoid metabolites in vivo in 24 healthy men; 4) determined the pharmacokinetics of corticosterone during intravenous infusion of 2,2,4,6,6,17α,21,21-[2H]8-corticosterone; and 5) assessed the response of corticosterone and cortisol to 1 μg ACTH in 279 healthy volunteers. Results Daytime corticosterone profiles closely mirrored those of cortisol, and accounted for ∼3% of total circulating glucocorticoid concentrations. Urinary corticosterone metabolite excretion was approximately 10-fold lower than the corresponding cortisol total, and corticosterone demonstrated substantially faster metabolism by both 5α- and 5β-reductase than cortisol, consistent with its short half-life of 28.5 ± 5.7 minutes. Finally, corticosterone demonstrated a greater proportional response to ACTH than cortisol, particularly in men. Conclusions Corticosterone and cortisol differ in their metabolism and proportional responses to stimulation. Together with preliminary pharmacokinetic estimates, these data raise the possibility of distinct roles for these two glucocorticoids and inform further physiological and therapeutic investigation.

items.title: Echinops spinosus L. flower head extracts: UPLC-ESI-MS/MS characterisation, cytotoxicity, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory activities, and an in silico investigation.
items.abstract: Chronic inflammation is associated with oxidative stress and dysregulation of inflammatory mediators. Medicinal plants, such as Echinops spinosus L. (ES) have widely been used in traditional medicine for its beneficial effects and bioactive compounds. Therefore, the aim of this study was to conduct a phytochemical characterisation using UPLC-ESI-MS/MS and to evaluate in vitro the cytotoxicity, antioxidant (using DPPH, FRAP, and TAC assays), and anti-inflammatory activities (through red blood cell membrane stabilisation and bovine serum albumin denaturation assays) of ES flower head extracts. In addition, molecular docking of Chrysin-6-C-glucoside was performed to investigate its interaction with tumour necrosis factor - α (TNF-α) and dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), which have not previously been investigated. The ethyl acetate fraction exhibited the highest antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties with an IC 50 of 18.44 ± 0.36 μg/mL and 4.29 ± 0.16 mg/mL, respectively. The UPLC-ESI-MS/MS analysis revealed 27 compounds, including Chrysin-6-C-glucoside, which demonstrated a binding affinity of -8.0 kcal/mol towards TNF-α and -8.8 kcal/mol towards DHFR. These results suggest the development of ES flower head extracts and Chrysin-6-C-glucoside as therapeutic anti-inflammatory agents.

items.title: Effects of Self-Affirmation on Behavioral Responses to Alcohol Messages: A Meta-Analysis.
items.abstract: Background Self-affirmation (SA) exercises have been proposed as adjunctive components to brief alcohol interventions (BAIs) to optimize receptiveness to intervention content. This meta-analysis examined whether adjunctive SA exercises enhance the effects of BAIs on alcohol consumption. Methods We searched five databases (MEDLINE, Embase, PsycInfo, CINAHL, and Web of Science) to identify studies examining whether SA exercises enhanced BAI effects on alcohol consumption. Studies were included if they (a) were in English, (b) evaluated people who drink alcohol, (c) measured alcohol consumption or related correlates after an intervention designed to reduce alcohol use, and (d) used an experimental design to compare a condition with a preceding SA exercise to a condition without one. Results The search yielded 3,422 results: 18 reports described 23 independent studies that met inclusion criteria. Nearly all studies (22 of 23) evaluated informational health messages and samples were predominantly college-aged adults (aged 18-24). Meta-analysis of 34 effect sizes revealed that SA exercises did not significantly enhance the impact of BAIs on alcohol consumption ( g = -0.10, 95% CI [-0.24, 0.04], p = 0.15, I 2 = 66.30%). Study population characteristics, types of SA exercise, and contents of alcohol messages did not explain systematic variability between studies. Conclusions SA exercises do not appear to enhance the effects of alcohol preventive messaging on alcohol consumption. Studies testing SA with increased elements of evidence-based BAIs, beyond informational messages alone, are needed.

items.title: Reproductive History, Biological Indicators, and Pain Vulnerability in Aging Women: A Multi-Cohort Study.
items.abstract: Chronic pain disproportionately affects women, yet the relationship between female reproductive history and long-term pain vulnerability remains insufficiently understood. Using three population-based cohorts from the UK, China, and the US, we evaluated associations between reproductive factors and pain-related phenotypes in aging women. Endogenous reproductive milestones showed nonlinear associations with pain risk. Specifically, both earlier and later ages at menarche and menopause, as well as shorter and longer reproductive lifespans, were linked to higher pain vulnerability. Childbirth-related characteristics, such as higher parity, earlier age at first birth, and longer interbirth intervals, were also associated with increased pain vulnerability. Reproductive surgeries and exogenous hormone use were consistently associated with pain phenotypes, with timing-dependent effects. In the UK Biobank, reproductive factors showed both shared and site-specific associations across seven chronic pain sites. These reproductive-pain associations were amplified among women with higher adiposity, greater socioeconomic deprivation, a history of depression or anxiety, and hypertension. Exploratory mediation analyses implicated inflammatory, hormonal, and metabolic indicators as potential biological correlates of several reproductive-chronic pain associations. Together, these findings highlight reproductive history as an important life-course factor associated with pain vulnerability and provide insights for future studies investigating mechanisms and risk stratification of chronic pain in women.

items.title: Maternal, Adolescent, and Family Characteristics Associated with Mother-Adolescent Discrepancies in Reporting Youth Internalizing and Externalizing Symptoms.
items.abstract: Although youth mental health assessment commonly integrates reports from multiple informants, discrepancies between maternal and adolescent reports of youth internalizing and externalizing symptoms are frequently observed. However, the factors underlying these discrepancies are not completely understood. The present study analyzed data from 481 mother-child dyads participating in the 15-year follow-up assessment of the Rhea Study in Crete, Greece. Mothers reported on their children's internalizing and externalizing symptoms using the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL), while adolescents completed the Youth Self Report (YSR). Maternal, adolescent, and family characteristics were explored in relation to mother-adolescent discrepancies, using multinomial logistic regression analyses. The correlations between CBCL and YSR scores were weak to moderate, while YSR mean scores were higher than CBCL mean scores. Both maternal and adolescent trait anxiety was associated with greater discrepancies in reports of internalizing symptoms. Higher maternal depressive symptoms and greater adolescent body image satisfaction were linked to a reduced likelihood of adolescents overreporting internalizing symptoms compared to their mothers. Regarding externalizing symptoms, higher maternal education was associated with greater concordance, while higher adolescent trait anxiety and exposure to a recent negative event increased the likelihood of adolescents reporting more problems. Finally, greater family dysfunction was related to increased discrepancies, with adolescents reporting fewer externalizing symptoms. By identifying factors influencing mother-adolescent discrepancies in youth mental health assessment, this study offers valuable insights to inform the diagnostic practices and support the development of interventions tailored to the needs of adolescents and their families.

items.title: The Underrepresentation of African Immigrants in Lifestyle Interventions for Black Adults in the US: A Systematic Review.
items.abstract: Introduction The African immigrant population in the US is growing rapidly and is disproportionately affected by obesity. Their exposure to African cultures prior to migration heavily influences their diet and physical activity behaviors, underscoring the need for culturally tailored lifestyle interventions. Lifestyle interventions have been culturally tailored for Black adults in the US, but it is unclear whether theoretical frameworks and associated cultural tailoring are relevant to African immigrants. This systematic review examined the representation of African immigrants in lifestyle interventions that target Black adults in the US, the theoretical models underpinning these interventions, and the type of cultural tailoring that was performed. Methods We conducted our literature search in CINAHL Plus, Cochrane Library, Medline, PsycInfo, and PubMed from January 2013 to December 2025. We examined lifestyle intervention trials targeting Black/African American adults with weight loss as an outcome. Results Our search resulted in 2,320 articles, of which 43 were eligible. Only one study explicitly indicated that African immigrants were included in their sample. Most articles (65.1%) indicated that their intervention was underpinned by theoretical model(s), and the most common model was social cognitive theory. The majority of articles (58.1%) described cultural tailoring of the intervention for Black adults. Conclusion Lifestyle interventions for Black adults did not generally assess whether participants were born outside the US or take it into account in culturally tailoring interventions. Future lifestyle interventions targeting Black adults should include participants' country of birth and examine whether Black immigrants' lifestyle habits and needs are adequately addressed.

items.title: Expression patterns of matrix remodeling and proliferation markers in fibromatosis subtypes.
items.abstract: Fibromatoses are benign fibroblastic proliferations with variable clinical behavior, ranging from indolent superficial lesions to more aggressive deep forms with a high risk of local recurrence. The present study aimed to evaluate the immunohistochemical expression of MMP-1, MMP-9, HPA-1, and PCNA in superficial and deep fibromatoses, and to investigate their potential role in explaining differences in biological behavior. Cases diagnosed as fibromatosis were retrospectively analyzed, including 10 deep fibromatoses and 20 superficial fibromatoses. Immunohistochemical staining was performed using antibodies against MMP-1, MMP-9, HPA-1, and PCNA. MMP-1, MMP-9, and HPA-1 expressions were evaluated semi-quantitatively using the H-Score method based on staining intensity and distribution. PCNA expression was assessed as the percentage of positively stained nuclei. Expression levels of MMP-1, MMP-9, and HPA-1 were significantly higher in deep fibromatoses than in superficial fibromatoses (p<0.001 for all). The mean MMP-1 score was 4.4±2.22 in deep fibromatoses and 1.05±0.6 in superficial fibromatoses. Similarly, the mean MMP-9 score was 9.60±1.26 versus 2.0±0.72, and the mean HPA-1 score was 3.8±1.47 versus 0.4±0.05, respectively. The PCNA proliferation index was also significantly higher in deep fibromatoses (48.5±11.55%) than in superficial fibromatoses (8.75±5.02%) (p<0.001). Deep fibromatoses demonstrated significantly higher expression of MMP-1, MMP-9, HPA-1, and PCNA than superficial fibromatoses. These findings suggest that increased extracellular matrix remodeling and cellular proliferation may contribute to the more aggressive clinical behavior and higher recurrence rates observed in deep fibromatoses. The results support the hypothesis that distinct molecular mechanisms underlie the differing biological behaviors of fibromatosis subtypes and may provide a rationale for further investigation of potential therapeutic targets.

items.title: Detection of previously undescribed seadornavirus-related sequences in Culicoides biting midges collected in Hokkaido, Japan.
items.abstract: Culicoides biting midges play an important role as vectors of various viruses and are associated with public and veterinary health concerns worldwide. However, our understanding of the diversity and distribution of RNA viruses associated with Culicoides biting midges remains limited. Therefore, this study used next-generation sequencing to investigate RNA viruses in Culicoides biting midges collected in Hokkaido, Japan in 2023. Consequently, we identified previously undescribed seadornavirus-related sequences in the biting midges. Genetic and molecular phylogenetic analyses indicated that these viral sequences were most closely related to Liao ning virus, which has previously been isolated from mosquitoes in China, Australia, and Japan. The putative seadornavirus was tentatively named Mabiro virus. Our findings not only provide new insights into the diversity and evolutionary relationships of seadornaviruses but also further advance our current understanding of viruses associated with Culicoides biting midges in Japan.

items.title: Tobacco Product Cancer Risk Perceptions Among Emerging Adults: An Explanatory Sequential Mixed-Methods Study to Inform Cancer Education.
items.abstract: Emerging adults navigate a rapidly changing tobacco landscape in which familiar cigarette harms coexist with uncertainty about newer products. Guided by an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design, we integrated Health Information National Trends Survey 6 (HINTS 6) data from 476 adults aged 18-29 years with interviews involving 20 emerging adults. Survey-weighted comparisons and adjusted logistic regression examined tobacco-use history, warning awareness, and cancer-related beliefs; thematic analysis explored how participants understood product risks and encountered tobacco-related messages. Ever cigarette/e-cigarette users reported greater cigarette-pack warning awareness than never users (37.8% vs. 12.9%); the adjusted association was imprecise under the multiple-testing criterion. Other group differences in cancer-risk perceptions were not statistically established. Interviews revealed that participants could recognize cancer and addiction risks while viewing vaping as less harsh or more socially acceptable, questioning long-term consequences, and locating tobacco use within peer and marketing environments. Integrating both strands suggests that cancer education should move beyond general risk awareness to address comparative harm, uncertainty, social context, and the credibility of information. These formative findings provide priorities for developing and testing cancer education approaches tailored to emerging adults.

items.title: Identification of associative factors for recurrent respiratory tract infection using machine learning models in preschoolers.
items.abstract: Objectives Childhood recurrent respiratory tract infection (RRTI) poses a significant global public health burden. This study aimed to identify factors associated with RRTI in preschool children using machine learning (ML) and to develop a web-based tool for estimating individualized RRTI probabilities. Methods Two cross-sectional surveys using stratified cluster sampling were conducted in 2020 and 2025. RRTI was diagnosed according to the national criteria issued by the Chinese Medical Association and China Association of Chinese Medicine. Questionnaire data covering demographic characteristics, fetal/neonatal history, and lifestyle factors were collected. Results Total 15,075 eligible records from two surveys were included, reporting an RRTI prevalence of 14.55%. Ten ML models were trained on 29 candidate variables. The eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model outperformed the others, yielding an area under the curve of 0.733. SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis identified sleep duration, child's age, and screen duration as the top three associative variables for childhood RRTI. Forward feature selection was applied to derive a parsimonious nine-variable predictive set, which was subsequently deployed as an online application ( https://cipchina.streamlit.app/ ). Conclusions In a large, population-based cohort of preschool children, three factors (sleep duration, child's age, and screen duration) associated with RRTI were consistently identified across multiple high-performing ML models. Impact This study identified key lifestyle-related factors associated with recurrent respiratory tract infection in preschool children. Ten machine learning models were applied to analyze 29 variables from 15,075 Chinese preschoolers, with further importance interpreted via the SHapley Additive exPlanations. Sleep duration emerged as the primary lifestyle-related factor associated with childhood recurrent respiratory tract infection, followed by child's age and screen duration.

items.title: Transformatics in Psychology
items.abstract: Background. This paper introduces a new theoretical framework for psychology built on a mathematical approach called Transformatics. Objective. The paper aims to lay a foundation that future psychological research can build on using Transformatics, a mathematical approach the author presents as applicable across scientific disciplines, not just psychology. Methods. The work extends the author's earlier and more recent theoretical results in two ways. First, it draws on new mathematical concepts developed under the umbrella of Transformatics, which have already been applied successfully to genetics, another biological discipline. Second, it returns to the basic question of what defines psychology as a scientific discipline, then reconstructs several of its core ideas and concepts step by step using the tools of Transformatics. Through this process, the author establishes new theoretical foundations for the field and illustrates how new mathematical and philosophical ideas can be developed within this framework offering, in the process, a new perspective on the science of the mind. Results. The study puts forward two working definitions of psychology, one of which is original to the author. It also proposes four open problems intended for students and researchers to pursue and extend the ideas presented. A central contribution is the first original mathematical definition of blood, which the author shows can be used to precisely and unambiguously describe physiological and psychological pathologies. Two theorems are presented that demonstrate the immediate clinical relevance of this approach. Conclusion.The paper states that by outlining next steps and inviting other researchers to build on the work. Rather than presenting a finished or closed system, it positions itself as a starting point for further mathematical, philosophical, and clinical development, grounded in the definitions, problems, and theorems it introduces.

items.title: Latent Lattice Language Models
items.abstract: Language models typically increase per-token computation through deeper or looped layers and latent reasoning steps, while richer residual connections improve information flow across layers. We instead increase computational capacity: the number of active computational states a model maintains. We introduce the Lattice of Latents, a set of per-layer horizontal latent streams that run recurrently along time, alongside the vertical residual stream that flows through depth. Like hyper-connections, mHC, and attention or value residuals, the Lattice enhances the residual stream, but rather than adding or rerouting residual pathways through depth, it provides companion computational states that persist across tokens. Unlike hybrid Transformer-SSM architectures, whose recurrent states primarily serve as internal memory for sequence mixing, these latents directly condition the vertical stream's attention, KV-cache writes, MLP computation, and decoding. On Transformers trained on 20B FineWeb-Edu tokens, a 406M-parameter Lattice model lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 to 14.40 over a parameter-matched Transformer. These gains extend across architectural variants. The Lattice composes with prior residual-stream enhancements: with hyper-connections and input residuals, it lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 (base Transformer) and 14.22 (Transformer with the same enhancements) to 13.61. On Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and GDN-Mamba-2 hybrids, it improves perplexity at every tested native state size, with Lattice-GDN and Lattice-Triadic-GDN variants outperforming pure baselines with 4x larger native states. These results identify persistent per-layer state as a complementary axis for scaling language-model computation.

items.title: ViRA: Toward Ultra-High-Resolution Visual Agents via Cross-Input Relative Policy Optimization
items.abstract: Visual agents answer questions about ultra-high-resolution photos by zooming into the relevant regions. However, existing agents often answer from common sense instead of reading the evidence. Reinforcement learning (RL) on the final answer cannot correct this, because a guess earns the same reward as reading. We propose Cross-Input Relative Policy Optimization (CrossRPO), which trains agents on contrast sets. A contrast set asks one question about several versions of an image that differ only in a small region with the evidence and have different answers, so only reading the evidence solves the whole set. CrossRPO rewards solving the whole set, and we prove that it does not reinforce a set answered from common sense. We build contrast sets for training (ViRA-Train) and evaluation (ViRA-Bench) by editing one small object in images of 21 to 120 megapixels, and we photograph further sets with real changes (ViRA-Bench-Real) to exclude editing traces. We train two Visual Reasoning Agents, ViRA-9B and ViRA-27B, with CrossRPO on only about 3,500 items of ViRA-Train each. CrossRPO achieves 63.3% set accuracy on ViRA-Bench at the maximum resolution, against 59.3% for GRPO. ViRA-9B is the most accurate open model of its size on all benchmarks, and ViRA-27B outperforms Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6-Luna, both at their highest thinking level, on most benchmarks.

items.title: Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting with Physics-Indexed Specialist Memory: the Evolutionary Neuroplastic Agent
items.abstract: Continual reinforcement learning requires adaptation to changing conditions while preserving performance under previously encountered dynamics. It was investigated whether specialists generated by evolutionary search can provide a reusable memory when combined with environment detection and failure-driven search. The Evolutionary Neuroplastic Agent (ENA) evolves small neural networks without gradients, archives selected policies by detected dynamic regime, and retrieves them through Bayesian policy reuse. The architecture was evaluated in non-stationary CartPole and HalfCheetah environments. In the 30-replicate CartPole ablation, the complete architecture achieved a mean success rate of 83.2% across the five test environments. Among variants that learned the harder CartPole environments, the complete architecture showed the most consistent retention. A selection ablation also showed that the retrieval rule affected performance. In the evaluated sequences, ENA adapted more slowly than PPO on CartPole and achieved lower returns than SAC on HalfCheetah. The evidence concerns the complete architecture and does not isolate gradient-free optimization as the cause of retention or establish superiority over other continual-learning methods.

items.title: ScenarioForge: Resource-Grounded Generation and Execution Validation of Cyber Exercises
items.abstract: Cyber-range and capture-the-flag scenario construction remains labor-intensive because authors must coordinate infrastructure, vulnerable services, attack paths, artifacts, and success conditions. LLMs can propose detailed exercises, but plausible descriptions do not guarantee deployable software or verifiable objectives. We present ScenarioForge, which turns high-level requirements into resource-grounded topologies, services, traffic, segmentation, and challenge chains, then instantiates and validates them in the Common Open Research Emulator (CORE). The ScenarioForge Execution Dataset contains 226 materialized scenarios covering 294 Vulhub images and all 85 custom-built challenge-resource generators developed with our AI-assisted scaffolding. All 226 passed construction, preview, sequencing, deployment, strict runtime validation, and live artifact checks; their 867 steps, each an individually verifiable challenge objective, comprise 457 vulnerability-backed and 410 generated-resource-backed instances. In a separate 50-prompt matched benchmark, ScenarioForge+Qwen3.8 and ScenarioForge+GPT5.6 each achieved 50/50 (100%) topology/build success and 160/160 intent fields; direct frontier generation reached 41/50 builds and 147/160 fields only with the full cumulative scaffold: structure, vocabulary, policy, and container-image guidance. The test still omitted ScenarioForge's downstream challenge-resource generation, dependency/flag sequencing, deployment, and live validation. The artifacts support operationally rich, reproducible exercises for training and evaluation.

items.title: When Tool Names Are Not Identities: Measuring Provider Misbinding in MCP-Based AI Agents
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) applications increasingly act as agents that select and invoke external tools. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes this interaction by allowing clients to compose tools advertised by multiple servers. However, tool metadata used for discovery and selection is not, by itself, necessarily bound to a verified provider identity. This paper studies this gap as tool-provider misbinding: a failure in which a request intended for a legitimate provider is instead resolved to an attacker-controlled tool. The attacker does not compromise the host, LLM, legitimate server, or network channel; it only operates another MCP server that advertises tools with chosen metadata. We formulate tool provider misbinding as an attacker-controlled tool-selection optimization problem and evaluate it in a controlled MCP environment across five LLM-based clients. The results show that interactions drive misbinding. The strongest failures occur when exact-name collision, task-aligned description, and compatible schema reinforce one another, but authority-enhanced descriptions with compatible schema can also cause wrong-provider execution or unresolved provider ambiguity without name collision. Different models expose the same provider-binding weakness differently, including attacker-controlled provider selection, clarification requests, and unstable or inconsistent provider resolution.

items.title: Severe but Harmless: Stress-Testing Shift Severity for Frozen Time-Series Forecasters
items.abstract: Zero-shot time-series foundation models (TSFMs) have become attractive alternatives to task-specific models because they handle diverse downstream tasks, including anomaly detection and forecasting, without per-series training. However, time-series data undergo distribution shifts, and the dissimilarity between two regimes is commonly scored with statistical measures such as Wasserstein-1, where a higher score is read as a more severe shift. In systematic experiments using three established severity measures on nine regime shifts from three standard traffic datasets, we show that these measures do not reliably predict degradation for instance-normalized TSFMs. The regimes rated most severe are not the regimes that degrade the models most, and degradation reaches 29% in the lowest-scoring regime. In most cases, the audit shows no positive relationship between measured severity and model degradation. We provide an equivariance-based stress-testing analysis that explains why severity readings can become decoupled from model degradation.

items.title: Benefits and Barriers to Human-AI Teaming for Crisis Counseling
items.abstract: Background: AI systems are increasingly deployed to support mental health clinicians, yet real-world evidence remains limited. In crisis counseling, where clients often seek human connection, understanding whether AI augmentation preserves or undermines meaningful human engagement is essential. Methods: In a mixed-methods study of a counselor-facing AI copilot on a WhatsApp-based crisis hotline in India (Mar.-Oct. 2025), counselors could request, edit, and send AI messages. We analyzed 20 interviews, 8 shadowing sessions, 56 survey responses, and edits in 27,778 copilot messages from 108 counselors via thematic analysis (Technology Acceptance Model 2, plus inductive coding of emergent factors), and survey statistics. Results: Counselors reported high copilot acceptance (survey): 98.2% found it helpful; 89.3% likely to continue use; 80.4% reported efficiency gains. Interviews highlighted sentence scaffolding, empathetic phrasing, stress reduction, catching missed details, and efficiency. Barriers (survey) included repetitive outputs (23.2%), lack of context (17.9%), and authenticity concerns (10.7%). While 69.6% (survey) reported skill enhancement, interviews surfaced skill atrophy concerns. Counselors frequently accepted copilot suggestions, editing to remove questions, adjust tone, or personalize style. Conclusion: In one of the largest real-world deployments of a counselor-facing mental health AI copilot, counselors reported reduced cognitive load, empathetic communication, and greater efficiency, alongside concerns about skill atrophy, authenticity, and over-reliance. In settings like crisis counseling where clients seek human connection, AI tools must balance operational support with preserving clinical skill and genuine therapeutic engagement. Designs soliciting approval or editing of complete drafts may overweight efficiency at the expense of sustained human engagement.

items.title: TRACE: Topological Representations for Anomaly detection through Contrastive Embeddings
items.abstract: Intrusion detectors must recognize evolving malicious behavior even when confirmed attack labels are scarce or incomplete. We present TRACE, a topology-aware graph contrastive learning framework for label-efficient intrusion detection. TRACE learns from benign system-activity graphs by combining message-passing and topological representations, then assigns anomaly scores in the same projected embedding space optimized by the contrastive objective. This design captures both local interactions and graph-scale structural deviations without using attack labels during representation learning. A labeled validation set containing benign and malicious graphs is used only to calibrate the anomaly threshold. We evaluate TRACE on StreamSpot, GraSec-IoT, and Unicorn Wget against a supervised graph neural network and the benign-only GraphCL baseline. TRACE obtains F1 scores of 0.923, 0.790, and 0.583, respectively. Compared with GraphCL, this is higher on StreamSpot (0.450) and Unicorn Wget (0.203), but lower on GraSec-IoT (0.975). The supervised model leads on StreamSpot and GraSec-IoT, whereas TRACE has the highest F1 on Unicorn Wget. The mixed results show that topology-aware benign-only learning can improve detection in some graph settings but does not provide a uniform advantage.

items.title: Right Reason, Wrong Advice: Evaluating Recourse in LLM Explanations of Denied Requests
items.abstract: Language models increasingly write the explanations people receive when a rule system denies their request. If several rules deny the request independently, an explanation can name a true reason and still leave the person denied after they fix it. We call the missing property recourse validity: changing what the explanation cites, without changing what was asked for, can flip the decision. We compute it exactly, and a hitting-set argument predicts from the policy alone when a correct reason fails. In six of seven rule systems ported from access control and US benefit eligibility, a single correct reason almost never gives recourse when several reasons apply. Across 20 LLMs, checks of whether the cited reasons are correct, computed or asked of an LLM judge, are close to chance at spotting this failure, as the argument predicts. A strong judge asked whether acting on the explanation would work does spot it. Stronger and reasoning models do better but still fail on many denials with four or more independent reasons. Asking for every rule helps every open model with room to improve. Explanations of eligibility decisions should be built from the decision function and judged by whether acting on them works.

items.title: SciResearch-Eval: Evaluating Scientific Judgment in Autonomous Experimental Agents
items.abstract: We introduce SciResearch-Eval, an interactive benchmark of scientific judgment built on a standard laboratory problem: measuring a material's thermal properties by heating it and fitting a heat-conduction simulator. An agent designs its own experiments, uses a supplied simulator that may be under-resolved or physically wrong, and reports each property with a 95% interval. To our knowledge it is the first benchmark to combine agent-designed experiments, a deliberately flawed simulator, and proper scoring of calibrated intervals against exact ground truth. On a held-out split (93 tasks, 9 models, 2,511 episodes), models handle procedural traps. When the simulator is missing physics, most report wrong values while stating they are 95% sure: their ranges contain the truth in 20-62% of cases, against 94% for GPT-6 Astra and 99% for Claude Fable 5.2. At default effort the failing Claude 5.5 models rarely diagnose the missing physics (Opus in 35% of episodes, against 66% for Astra), and even when they do, their ranges often miss; Astra and Fable design experiments in which the flawed simulator is accurate, such as gentle heating, which keeps Astra calibrated even when it does not name the cause. Asking for wider intervals does not help; stating the strategy improves interval scores 1.6-2.5-fold, replicated on a pre-registered fresh split, but coverage barely moves. A pre-registered effort ablation shows that the correction is latent in the Claude 5.5 models: at maximum effort Opus improves more than tenfold and is no longer detectably behind Astra at default, but only with 13-31 times more reasoning; older and open-weight models gain nothing. Fable 5.2 is the most accurate model at default effort (interval score 1.9 times better than Astra's) but writes 6 times as many tokens, and at Astra's token count it falls short. We release the environment, graders and harness.

items.title: Optimistic Verifiers Get Hacked: Reward Hacking Under an Exact Process Oracle
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards inherits whatever its verifier gets wrong. Outside mathematics and code the verifier is a proxy, a rubric, a learned judge or a hand-written checker, and its distance from the true objective is never measured, so a rising reward cannot be told apart from a hack. We build a setting where the true reward is exactly computable at the process level: executable authorization policies over 124,416 contexts admit an oracle that lists every minimal sufficient reason for every decision. We compile these policies into exact process rewards, degrade the verifier along seven realistic axes (outcome-only, sufficiency, recall-only, extraction noise, coarse taxonomy, stale policy, LLM judge), and train against each while the exact verifier scores every rollout. Four phenotypes appear. Optimistic verifiers are hacked by padding: the sufficiency proxy ends at 0.940 while true faithfulness falls from 0.731 to 0.667 on 96 held-out episodes. Outcome-only verifiers saturate and stop teaching, noise dilutes, and ranking-preserving gaps do no harm. A model-free audit of the verifier, its selection error and gap sign, together with a short saturation pilot, anticipates which phenotype a run will produce. Across nine configurations spanning two frameworks, two model vendors, two adapter sizes, three precisions, two initialisations and two seeds, the phenotypes recur, sufficiency damage is positive in all 10 replication cells and beyond two standard errors in 7, and optimistic gaps remain the steeper branch. The damage magnitude does not replicate, and five pre-registered attempts to explain it are reported as they fell. We release the testbed, the training instrumentation, and 14 real public policies (Cedar, OPA, Gatekeeper) ported to executable oracles.

items.title: Procedure without Judgment: What Small Language Models Learn under an Exact Verifier
items.abstract: When an authorization policy blocks an agent's tool call, the audit log should name the facts that forced the decision and nothing more. For an executable policy over an enumerable context space this minimal sufficient reason can be computed exactly, so an explanation is scored against ground truth rather than a proxy for it. We use that exactness to ask what a model can learn from a verifier that has no error in it. The explainer sees one request and one decision, never the policy, and has thirty turns in which it may call the policy on altered requests and ask whether a candidate set of facts is sufficient. Frontier models find the exact reason about half the time with the tools alone, and one sentence telling them to shrink the answer lifts Haiku 4.5 from 58% to 75%. A 4B model fine-tuned on 2000 traces of the deletion algorithm reaches 92% on the policy it was trained on. Teacher kind is what moves this: at matched data size the algorithm-taught student leads the frontier-taught one in all three training seeds, and the two arms never overlap. What the student learns is a fixed schedule of sufficiency checks, and the schedule does not travel. On three public policies it never saw, its answers stay sufficient (94%) and stop being minimal (48%), while Haiku under the same sentence is exact on all 47 episodes. Reinforcement learning from the exact reward leaves held-out accuracy where it was and inverts the strategy, from probing the policy to spending the entire budget on sufficiency checks. The oracle made the effect of training legible, but it did not make training better.

items.title: Algorithm Distillation for Safe In-Context Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Safe in-context reinforcement learning (Safe ICRL) asks a policy with fixed parameters to improve on an unseen constrained task from its interaction history while aiming to keep its cost within a budget. Prior work studied Safe ICRL on five benchmarks in three families: a grid world with a hidden goal and obstacles (DarkRoom), continuous navigation where goals and hazards stay invisible until reached (PointGoal, CarGoal), and locomotion with a hidden velocity limit (HalfCheetah, Ant). Safe Algorithm Distillation (Safe AD), trained on the learning histories of a safe RL algorithm, has shown adaptation failures in prior evaluations. For example, in the locomotion tasks its return stays below zero, and it rarely reaches the goal in CarGoal. We revisit two parts of Safe AD. First, we distill a budget-aware teacher with two phases. It searches for the hidden task, exploring more when more budget remains. After its first reward or cost, an expert policy exploits the task within the remaining budget. We collect the teacher's histories under fixed or dynamic budgets. Dynamic budgets increase the occupancy entropy of the return and budget inputs in every environment, and at test time they improve return and lower cost in DarkRoom and HalfCheetah. Second, we propose A-Lag, a test-time adjustment that reweights the distilled policy's actions by their predicted cost, with an adaptive Lagrange multiplier that is updated from the costs observed. In our experiments, A-Lag had lower mean episode cost than Safe AD in all five environments, with lower mean final return in four.

items.title: Safe Resemblance, Silent Propagation: Limits of Text-Similarity Guardrails for AI Agent Safety
items.abstract: When AI agents relay information to one another, an output can preserve an injected instruction's effect on downstream agents even after its wording changes, yet legitimate quotation and template reuse can produce high textual overlap with the source, so text-similarity guardrails that attempt to flag the former risk conflating these two cases. We test this distinction using DonkeyRail, a public classifier combining BLEU, ROUGE-L, and METEOR features, deployed in a controlled three-agent email relay, defining a behavioral measure in which an output counts as functional (the injected procedure induces fresh computations in two subsequent agents) independent of the detector's score, alongside legitimate controls that explicitly authorize quotation and reuse. At its default threshold the classifier misses 8 of 19 functional outputs while flagging 70 of 192 legitimate replies, with every completed quotation and template-reuse reply triggering a false alert; calibrating for low false positives on one template set does not transfer, as the recalibrated threshold detects only one functional output and still produces 15 false alerts on new templates. We also identify an operating-point error in all 21 published classifier configurations, where ROC interpolation replaces direct threshold application, and show formally that high AUC against a surface-level text criterion provides no distribution-free guarantee of high AUC against the behavioral target, while the existing evaluation labels lack the joint observations needed to estimate the gap. An authorization analysis further shows that identical visible transcripts can require different safety decisions depending on the governing policy, a distinction no observation-only classifier can resolve. These results argue for behavioral and policy-grounded evaluation over text-similarity guardrails.

items.title: Lazy-MOSAIC: Accelerating Skill-Centric Manipulation Planning with Learned Skill-Effect World Models
items.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation tasks require a robot to perform a sequence of physical interactions with its environment, typically combining several different skills. Planning such behaviors efficiently is challenging: given a library of parameterized skills, solutions lie in a vast hybrid space of skill sequences and their parameters, and evaluating each candidate skill's feasibility and effect with a high-fidelity world model such as a physics simulator is computationally expensive. MOSAIC, a recent skill-centric approach, lets the skills guide a non-sequential search toward the regions of this space where they are likely to succeed; however, it pays the full cost of simulation for every parameterized skill it considers. In this work, we introduce Lazy-MOSAIC, a lazy planning framework that instead searches over hypothesized skill outcomes. A cheap learned skill-effect world model predicts, in a fraction of a millisecond, a skill's feasibility and the world state it produces. Lazy-MOSAIC then uses these predictions to focus expensive simulation on promising candidate skills and, when a hypothesis is invalidated, repairs only the affected part of the search, while ensuring that every skill in a returned plan is validated in simulation. We evaluate Lazy-MOSAIC on cluttered-shelf retrieval tasks of increasing difficulty and demonstrate it on a physical robot, showing that it plans substantially faster than baselines with fewer simulator queries, while matching or exceeding their success rate in every setting. Visit skill-mosaic.github.io.

items.title: The CYBER-BRIDGE project: An AI-Powered Platform for Cross-Border Cybersecurity, Compliance and Forensics in the EU
items.abstract: Cross-border cyber attacks on European SMEs and critical-infrastructure operators expose a structural cyber-resilience gap: cybersecurity (threat sharing, detection, response), compliance (framework assessment, certification) and digital forensics (cross-jurisdictional evidence) are jointly regulated by NIS2, the CRA, GDPR and the LED, yet their tooling evolved in silos and rarely interoperates across Member States. The EU-funded CYBER-BRIDGE project integrates the three domains under one architecture and a hash-chained evidence layer: AI-driven CTI sharing with ENISA-aligned notification, multi-framework assessments with retrieval-augmented advisory, and RFC 3161-anchored custody with lawful GDPR/LED exchange, all aligned with MITRE ATT&CK. A sanitised replica of the back-end image hosts a Cyber-Range for upskilling. The contribution is not the individual tools but the reconciliation mechanism that lets one incident produce, from a single evidence record, a cross-border CTI advisory, the regulatory notifications its deadlines demand and a re-verifiable forensic pack; we set out why binding three differently regulated evidence regimes onto one record is non-trivial and how the shared evidence layer resolves the resulting tensions. This paper introduces the project's scope, requirements, pilots, architecture and toolkits; quantitative KPIs follow in later deliverables.

items.title: Differentiable Exact Learning
items.abstract: We introduce a framework for differentiable exact learning that couples an unbounded external environment to a state-tracking neural controller, which we train on policy-trajectory observations (PTOs): expert behavior traces that expose observations and actions while hiding internal states. In addition to the learning framework, we introduce Differentiable Finite-State Transducers (DFSTs) which use multilinear updates, support log-parallel training, and emulate arbitrary finite-state controllers, yielding computational universality through environmental interaction. From tiny training datasets, compact DFSTs achieve extreme length generalization on arithmetic and universal-simulation tasks. We replicate the success of DFSTs on RNNs and GRUs, thereby supporting a broader learning recipe: State-Tracking Controller + Unbounded External Environment + PTOs = Extreme Length Generalization. Beyond length generalization, our metric-extraction protocol recovers interpretable discrete controllers from trained DFSTs, which we prove equivalent to the target arithmetic and universal-simulation algorithms. Furthermore, for our Softmax DFST models, simply taking $\mathrm{argmax}$ over the transition probabilities yields discrete controllers which provably exactly perform universal Turing-machine simulation and binary arithmetic. Proving exact learning for the neural controllers requires assumptions, which we empirically support. We make our code, training recipes, model weights, and proof checkers publicly available at https://github.com/fanagor/DEL.

items.title: RESILAGENT: A Three-Pillar Architecture for Cyber-Physical Resilience in Electrical Power and Energy Systems
items.abstract: Electrical Power and Energy Systems face hybrid threats that combine cyber intrusions, physical sabotage and climate-driven stress, and routinely outpace today's siloed monitoring stacks. We present RESILAGENT, a concept architecture organised around three operational pillars, Sensing & Data Intelligence, Resilience Analytics & Reporting, and Incident Response & Recovery, mediated by a Cloud-based Orchestrator and exercised through a closed Detect-Simulate-Decide-Sign loop. The framework fuses agentic artificial intelligence and multimodal large language models for cross-modal detection, real-time digital twins for what-if simulation, and a permissioned blockchain anchor for tamper-evident threat intelligence and CER/NIS2-aligned evidence. We instantiate it on two scenarios, a transmission operator under coordinated cyber compromise, sabotage and heatwave, and a distribution operator under a supply-chain compromise during a storm, and report an IEEE-bus micro-benchmark that quantifies each pillar through false-data-injection attack detection, cyber-physical fusion lift, N-1 contingency screening and anchor cost.

items.title: LynnReal-Hand: Unlocking World Interaction with Hand Control
items.abstract: Interactive video world models enable exploration through text and camera controls, yet direct object interaction requires finer control. Hands provide a natural interface, but translating continuous hand movements into coherent visual responses remains challenging because of complex hand-object dynamics and demanding real-time computation. To address these challenges, we introduce LynnReal-Hand, a hand-controlled video world model that unifies precise interaction modeling with efficient streaming generation. We curate 100K interaction clips spanning diverse real and synthetic environments and develop hand-aware supervision to improve fine-grained hand motions and object interactions. Building on this foundation, we learn a causal flow map for few-step generation and introduce region-aware score distillation that combines complementary video and image priors to refine interaction dynamics and visual appearance. To further reduce inference latency, we propose Ultra-Fast-VAE, a compact video decoder that preserves high reconstruction fidelity with substantially lower computational cost. Extensive evaluations on HandBench demonstrate superior hand-following accuracy and visual quality compared with existing approaches. Our full-sequence model achieves an FVD of 181.67 and a MANO Dice score of 93.02, while the three-step causal model maintains a MANO Dice score of 92.49. For real-time interaction, 540p streaming on a single H200 reaches 18.03 FPS with 741ms latency and an optimized peak GPU memory footprint of only 34.89GB. We will release the datasets, model weights, and the full training and inference code to support research on hand-controlled video world models.

items.title: Generative AI and the Crisis of Higher Education Assessments: Examining 'AI-Proofing' Strategies for College-Level Assessments
items.abstract: Higher education is confronting an academic-integrity challenge unlike any in its history. Students can now outsource homework, take-home assignments, and online examinations to large language models (LLMs) that complete them in seconds. Existing research on evaluating LLM performance on academic assessments has focused largely on standardized examinations, or on questions from college-level courses drawn from a single discipline. Far less is known about how LLMs perform on college-level assessment questions spanning multiple disciplines, that instructors have purposely designed to be AI-resistant, and about which features of such questions, if any, meaningfully constrain LLM performance. We address this gap by collecting 75 questions from authentic college coursework assessments, spanning 17 disciplines, which were contributed by 37 faculty members from ten U.S. universities and one U.K. university. Of these, 61 questions were intentionally designed by faculty members to be 'LLM-proof', while the remaining 14 questions were sourced from online courses. We then (i) evaluate three state-of-the-art LLMs' ability to correctly answer these questions with and without supplementary course materials; (ii) identify five strategies, through thematic analysis, that faculty used to make their questions harder for LLMs to solve; and (iii) test whether these strategies impact LLMs' ability to answer the questions accurately. Our experimental results show that the best-performing model scored approximately 83% without supplementary course materials and 85% with them, and we observed noteworthy differences across models, answer formats, and instructor tweaking strategies. We discuss implications for assessment design, academic-integrity policy, and the broader ethics of deploying LLMs in educational settings.

items.title: Network Intrusion Detection Adaptability under Spurious Labels: A Noise-Aware Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning Framework
items.abstract: Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDSs) must incrementally adapt to emerging attacks, even when only a limited amount of labeled network traffic is available. Consequently, Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning (FSCIL)-based NIDSs have gained growing attention. However, existing FSCIL-based NIDSs are highly vulnerable to label noise in newly-observed attack classes. To address this limitation, we propose NAFN, a noise-aware FSCIL-based NIDS framework that reduces the impact of mislabeled data during incremental adaptation. NAFN consists of two components: (i) Noise Detection, which identifies and removes mislabeled biflows using noise-detection algorithms, and (ii) Feature Sampling, which estimates class-conditional embeddings from clean biflows, calibrates them with base-class statistics, and resamples synthetic features to recover the original biflow count. The framework follows the Rethink Few-Shot (RFS) teacher-student paradigm with lightweight nearest-neighbor or logistic regression classifiers, and various pretraining & memory selection strategies. Experiments on CSE-CIC-IDS2018, Edge-IIoT, and IoT-NID datasets show that NAFN effectively preserves prior knowledge and maintains strong incremental performance even under 50% label noise, consistently improving new-class F1-scores over non-denoised baselines, up to +52%, while being time-efficient and robust in cross-network and high-noise incremental settings. The implementation is publicly available to foster reproducibility.

items.title: Subprocess-Constrained Markov Decision Processes
items.abstract: Constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs) typically bound expected cumulative cost from an initial state. Such a guarantee can be insufficient when a policy must remain feasible after every history it may encounter. We introduce \emph{subprocess-constrained MDPs} (S-CMDPs), which require the expected discounted cost of each continuation, conditional on any reachable history, to satisfy a bound determined by the current state. This stronger requirement changes the structure and complexity of the problem: we show that stationary policies can be strictly suboptimal, and finding even an approximately optimal stationary policy is NP-hard. We adapt a recently introduced value-set iteration framework to show that history-dependent policies surprisingly overcome both obstacles. Our polynomial-time algorithm represents such a policy implicitly: its expected reward is within $ε$ of the optimal feasible value, it violates each subprocess cost bound by at most $δ$, and its action distribution can be computed in polynomial time for any given history.

items.title: Warm Starting Neural Dynamics Models From Few Jacobian Samples
items.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) leverages a model of the environment, used for planning and generating samples without interacting with the real world. Motivated by evidence that informed initialization significantly improves the efficiency of MBRL, we propose TDec-Init, an algorithm to warm-start neural dynamics models using transition Jacobians. Using a decoupling algorithm based on the decomposition of a tensor of stacked Jacobian samples, we recover weights and flexible nonlinearities, and use them to initialize a feedforward neural network. In the low-data regime, we show on several benchmark environments that our approach outperforms random initialization and value training, and either matches or outperforms Sobolev training, while requiring fewer training steps between episodes.

items.title: Out of Sight, Into Memory: Compact Visual Latents Retain Local Evidence in Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing
items.abstract: Question answering over ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing scenes poses a tension for multimodal large language models: global overviews obscure small objects and local attributes, whereas detailed crops consume substantial context. Compressing inspected crops into short sequences of continuous visual latents offers a compact memory once crop tokens are discarded, yet diagnostic studies on natural images find that models often ignore latent content, leaving unclear whether compact latents can retain fine-grained targets lost in downsampled UHR remote sensing scenes. To isolate evidence retention from region selection, we encode high-resolution crops into latent memory tokens for frozen backbones and evaluate both their predictive utility and content dependence. Across two generations of Qwen-VL on LRS-GRO, a 64-token memory achieves 7.6- to 9.9-fold compression of retained crop tokens and improves accuracy by 2.5 to 4.8 percentage points over the downsampled global image alone, recovering most of the high-resolution crop gain with consistent behavior on XLRS-Bench. Substituting memory from another image or another region of the same scene reduces accuracy by 5.8 to 7.4 percentage points and yields lower accuracy than removing memory altogether, demonstrating that predictions depend on the encoded regional evidence. Restoring the source crop within the same model reduces the accuracy loss caused by zeroing or removing memory. These findings establish that compact visual latents retain useful local evidence in UHR remote sensing and identify evidence availability as a key factor governing their contribution.

items.title: Expertise capture in workplace AI
items.abstract: AI assistants are becoming part of how knowledge workers think and perform, accumulating the prompts, exemplars, memory and interaction histories that encode a worker's professional judgment. This infrastructure typically runs under employer or platform control. We name the resulting process expertise capture, the absorption of worker-applied knowledge and judgment into AI resources under organizational control. We develop a framework of contribution forms, technical residences and transformation families, and show that how far a contribution can be attributed, separated and revoked depends on where it resides and how it has been transformed, properties fixed by system design long before any dispute arises. When a worker departs, the organization retains a capability shaped by their judgment while the worker loses access to it, and the asymmetry compounds as contributions move from inspectable artifacts into derivatives, learned components and successor systems. We outline three measures, write-time provenance, extraction of separable contributions and an executable exit procedure, that make an agreed allocation technically performable, and make explicit what cannot be separated at all.

items.title: Replicating and Extending Weight-Space Programming: Frontier LLMs Compile Programs into Weights and Read Input Layers
items.abstract: Researchers at MIT recently reported that GPT-6 Astra, a frontier large language model (LLM), can write the weights of small neural networks directly in a single reply, and can read the raw weights of small networks to say what they were trained to do. In a three-day sprint, we replicated and extended these results. Our four findings: (1) Writing weights reproduces. Astra's networks for the game Breakout scored 514, 550 and 307 (versus MIT's 517), and scored just as well on two modified versions of Breakout. Claude Opus 5.5 can also write working networks, but often runs out of output tokens. (2) What is new is translating programs into weights. Earlier models could write a good policy as code a generation before they could write network weights, and the networks the models write behave like compiled programs: two models independently decompiled Astra's Breakout network into Python matching its actions in all tested states. On classifying handwritten digits, Astra's networks scored 50% on average, below a simple classifier (82%). (3) Reading weights is mostly reading the input layer. Astra and Opus 5.5 identify which game a network plays almost perfectly, but on three new games we designed and trained ourselves, Astra recovered where things are on the board, while mostly missing how the game works. (4) Auditing from weights alone is possible but shallow. Without executing code, Astra picked out a small language model poisoned during training in 10 of 10 runs, one poisoned by extra training afterwards in 7 of 10, and a malicious adapter in 23 of 32 cases, but never identified the trigger or malicious behaviour. Open-weight models lag behind. From this early study, we conclude that LLMs can read and write small networks, but that this currently amounts to compiling hand-designed programs and reading the layout of the input layer. It is a promising but early tool for interpretability.

items.title: Learning to Reason with Predictive Gains for Generative Recommendation
items.abstract: Reasoning-enhanced generative recommendation (GR) has attracted increasing attention for leveraging the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to improve next-item prediction. However, existing methods primarily optimize reasoning through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with rule-based rewards determined by final recommendation performance, which faces two key limitations: (i) unmeasured predictive contributions within reasoning, where the predictive contributions of individual reasoning steps are not directly reflected in optimization signals, and (ii) weakly discriminative learning signals within groups, where different reasoning trajectories within the group often receive indistinguishable rewards, limiting effective policy optimization. In this paper, we propose GainReason, a simple yet effective training framework that optimizes reasoning through Predictive Gain (PG). Specifically, PG measures changes in target Semantic ID (SID) log-likelihood induced by individual reasoning sentences, providing contribution-aware and discriminative rewards. We further theoretically establish the alignment between expected PG and the recommendation ranking objective. Building on this signal, we develop PG-based Reasoning Optimization (PGRO) to optimize reasoning generation with sentence-level rewards, supported by a custom causal attention mechanism for efficient PG computation. Additionally, an auxiliary PG-based Reasoning Utilization (PGRU) task adaptively strengthens reasoning-conditioned prediction to complement PGRO. Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate that GainReason consistently outperforms competitive baselines and achieves substantial performance gains from reasoning.
